history.meaning: to start shining, light up, beam

зато.etymology: Fused adversative conjunction from the prepositional phrase за то ('in exchange for that, to make up for that'), combining за ('for, in exchange for') + то ('that', neuter of тот).

history.meaning: on the bright side, on the other hand, to make up for it

защитный.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -ный from защита ('protection, defence'), a deverbal noun from защитить ('to protect, shield'), built on prefix за- ('behind') + щит ('shield', from Proto-Slavic *ščitъ): literally 'placing behind a shield'.

заявление.etymology: Verbal noun formed from заявить ('to declare, announce, state officially'), built from the prefix за- and явить ('to show, manifest, make public', from Proto-Slavic *javiti 'to make manifest').

history.meaning: to declare → official statement, written application, police report

звонко.etymology: Adverbial form in -о of звонкий ('clear-ringing, resonant, voiced'), formed from звон ('ringing sound, peal of bells', from Old East Slavic звонъ and Proto-Slavic *zvonъ).

здорово.etymology: Formed from the neuter short form of здоровый ('healthy, robust, big, fine'), inherited from Old East Slavic съдоровъ (displaying East Slavic pleophony -оро-), from Proto-Slavic *sъdorvъ ('made of good wood, sound, healthy', from *sъ- 'good' + *dervo 'tree, wood'). With stress on the first syllable (**здо́рово**), it functions as an enthusiastic colloquial evaluation ('great, cool, awesome!'); with stress on the second syllable (**здоро́во**), it is a colloquial greeting ('hi, hello!').

здоровье.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic съдоровье (showing East Slavic pleophony -оро-), formed with the abstract neuter suffix -ье (*-ьje) from съдоровъ / здоровый ('healthy, sound'), from Proto-Slavic *sъdorvъ ('of good wood/timber, robust', from *sъ- 'good' + *dervo 'tree, wood').
здоровье.notes: Used in the standard toast **За здоровье!** ('To your health!') and in **На здоровье!** ('You're welcome!', said in reply to thanks for food or hospitality).

здравствуй.etymology: Second-person singular imperative of здравствовать ('to be in good health, thrive'), formed on the Old Church Slavonic stem здрав- (corresponding to native East Slavic здоров- in здоровый), from Proto-Slavic *sъdorvъ ('sound, healthy'). Literally, здравствуй! is a wish meaning 'be healthy!'.

history.meaning: healthy → to be in good health

здравствуй.notes: The first **в** is silent in pronunciation: **[здра́ствуй]**.

здравствуйте.etymology: Grammatically the formal plural imperative of здравствовать ('to thrive, be in good health'), so greeting someone with Здравствуйте! literally wishes 'be healthy!'. The root здрав- is the Church Slavonic counterpart of native East Slavic здоров- (здоровый), from Proto-Slavic *sъdorvъ ('sound, sturdy', literally 'of good wood', built on *sъ- 'good' + *dervo 'tree, timber').

history.meaning: healthy → to be in good health

здравствуйте.notes: Pronounced with a silent first в (sounded like 'zdrastvuyte'). Use singular *Здравствуй* with one close friend or relative.

зеркало.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic зеркало (alongside Church Slavonic зерцало), from Proto-Slavic *zьrkadlo, built from the gaze root *zьrěti ('to look, behold') plus the tool suffix *-dlo (regularly becoming -ло in East Slavic): literally 'a looking-tool'.

злой.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic зълъ (long form зълыи), from Proto-Slavic *zъlъ ('bad, evil, angry, crooked'), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰwel- ('to bend, curve, deviate from the right path'; compare Lithuanian Pa-žulnùs 'sloping, crooked', Avestan zūrah- 'deceit, wrong', and Sanskrit hválati 'goes astray').

знак.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic знакъ and Old Church Slavonic знакъ ('sign, token, mark'), formed with the suffix *-kъ from Proto-Slavic *znati ('to know, recognize', from Proto-Indo-European *ǵneh₃-): literally 'that by which something is known or recognized'.

знаменитый.etymology: Inherited via Old Church Slavonic знаменитъ ('marked, distinguished, renowned'), formed with the adjectival suffix -итый from знамя (stem знамен-, from Old East Slavic знамя, genitive знамене 'mark, sign, banner', built on Proto-Slavic *znati 'to know').

значит.etymology: Originally the third-person singular present tense ('it means, it signifies') of значить ('to mean, signify'), derived from знак ('sign, mark', from Proto-Slavic *znakъ / *znati 'to know'). Used parenthetically in conversation as 'so, then, that means'.

золотистый.etymology: Adjective formed with the colour/hue suffix -истый ('having the sheen or tint of') from золото ('gold'), inherited from Old East Slavic золото (with East Slavic pleophony -оло-) and Proto-Slavic *zolto (cognate with English gold).

morphemes.meaning: having the tint or lustre of

зря.etymology: Historically the fossilized present active participle (gerund) of the archaic verb зреть ('to look, see', Old East Slavic зьрѣти, Proto-Slavic *zьrěti). In the phrase не зря ('not looking blindly, not without reason'), зря shifted by back-formation or from 'just looking on idly / at random without thinking' to its modern meaning 'in vain, for nothing, pointlessly'.

history.meaning: at random, without thinking → in vain, for nothing

зуб.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic зубъ (and Old Church Slavonic зѫбъ), from Proto-Slavic *zǫbъ ('tooth'), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵómbʰos ('peg, row of teeth, tooth', from *ǵembʰ- 'to bite, snap'; exact cognate with Ancient Greek γόμφος 'peg, molar', Sanskrit jámbha- 'tooth, tusk', Lithuanian žam̃bas 'sharp edge', and English comb).

игра.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic игра ('game, play, dance, festivity'), from Proto-Slavic *jьgra ('play, game, dance'). Deeper Indo-European etymology is debated (Vasmer discusses proposed connections to Sanskrit éjati 'stirs, moves' and Old Norse eikinn 'wild, lively').

идиот.etymology: Borrowed via French idiot or German Idiot (and Late Latin idiōta 'uneducated person, layman') from Ancient Greek ἰδιώτης (idiṓtēs, 'private citizen not holding public office; layman, unskilled person'), derived from ἴδιος (ídios, 'one's own, private').

history.meaning: private → private citizen, layman, ignorant person

идти.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic ити (present иду), from Proto-Slavic *iti, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁éyti ('to go'; compare Latin īre and Lithuanian eĩti). Its past tense шёл, шла, шли comes from a separate suppletive Slavic stem *šьd- (related to ходить).

из-под.etymology: Compound preposition formed in East Slavic by combining из ('out of, from inside', from Proto-Slavic *jьz) + под ('under', from Proto-Slavic *podъ). Governs the genitive case to express motion 'from under' or a container that formerly held something (банка из-под чая 'an empty tea tin').

history.meaning: from under; formerly holding (of a container)

известный.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic извѣстьнъ ('known for certain, well-known, reliable'), derived from извѣсть / вѣсть ('news, knowledge, message', Russian весть), from Proto-Slavic *věstь (built on *věděti 'to know', PIE *weyd-).

изменить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic измѣнити (and Old Church Slavonic измѣнити 'to exchange, alter'), formed from из- ('out') + мѣнити ('to change, exchange', from мѣна 'exchange, alternation', Proto-Slavic *měna). With an accusative object (изменить план), it means 'to change, alter'; with a dative object (изменить мужу / родине), it means 'to betray, be unfaithful to, cheat on'.

history.meaning: to change (+ acc.); to betray, cheat on (+ dat.)

измениться.etymology: Perfective reflexive/intransitive verb formed by adding -ся to изменить ('to change, alter'), derived from из- + менить (from Proto-Slavic *měna 'change, exchange').

изумительный.etymology: Adjective formed with the suffix -тельный from изумить ('to amaze, astonish'), literally 'to take someone out of their mind with wonder' (built on prefix из- 'out of' + ум 'mind, wit', from Proto-Slavic *umъ).

history.meaning: out of + mind → to astonish → amazing, exquisite, wonderful

икра.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic икра ('fish roe, caviar; calf of the leg'), from Proto-Slavic *jьkra ('roe, spawn; rounded mass'), cognate with Lithuanian ikrai ('fish roe, spawn').

иметь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic имѣти (and Old Church Slavonic имѣти), from Proto-Slavic *iměti ('to have, hold'), a stative verb built on the same Indo-European root as *jęti ('to take', compare Latin emō 'to take, buy'). Unlike Western European languages, Russian generally expresses everyday possession with у меня есть rather than иметь, reserving иметь for abstract and formal collocations.
иметь.notes: Used chiefly in set phrases such as **иметь право** ('to have the right'), **иметь в виду** ('to mean, have in mind'), and **иметь значение** ('to matter').

иначе.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic инако / иначе ('otherwise, in another way'), comparative/adverbial formation from инъ / иной ('other, another'), from Proto-Slavic *inъ ('one, other', cognate with Latin ūnus and English one).
иначе.notes: Both stress patterns are accepted in standard Russian: **и́наче** and **ина́че** (with **так или ина́че** 'one way or another' always stressed on the middle syllable).

инвалид.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century (originally referring to disabled war veterans, on the model of Paris's Hôtel des Invalides) from French invalide ('infirm, disabled soldier'), from Latin invalidus ('weak, infirm, powerless'), formed from in- ('not') + validus ('strong, healthy', from valēre 'to be strong').

history.meaning: disabled veteran → person with a disability

интересный.etymology: Formed with the Russian adjectival suffix -ный from интерес ('interest'), borrowed in the Petrine era via German Interesse (or French intérêt) from Medieval Latin interesse ('to be of importance, make a difference; compensation').

history.meaning: to be between, make a difference, matter

интересовать.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century (modeled on French intéresser and German interessieren) from интерес ('interest') + the verbal suffix -овать, ultimately from Latin interesse ('to be between, make a difference, concern, be of importance').

history.meaning: to concern, be of importance → to interest

интернет.etymology: Borrowed in the 1990s from English Internet, shortened from internetwork ('interconnected network of computer networks'), formed from the Latin prefix inter- ('between, among') + English network.

информация.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via Polish informacja or German Information from Latin īnfōrmātiō ('outline, concept, instruction, explanation'), derived from īnfōrmāre ('to shape, fashion, instruct, educate', from in- 'into' + fōrma 'form, shape').

history.meaning: to give form to, instruct → concept, instruction

искатель.etymology: Agent noun formed with the suffix -тель from искать ('to seek, look for, search'), inherited from Old East Slavic искати and Proto-Slavic *jьskati (cognate with English ask and Lithuanian ieškoti 'to seek').

искренне.etymology: Adverb formed from искренний ('sincere, heartfelt'), which goes back to Old East Slavic and Old Church Slavonic искрьнии ('near, neighboring, close, intimate'), derived from the archaic adverb/preposition искрь ('near, close by'). The deeper origin of *jьz-krь connects to *krai / *krь ('edge, side', compare край): originally 'standing right beside one, close at hand', whence 'intimate, open-hearted, sincere'.

history.stage: Old Church Slavonic / Old East Slavic

искусство.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic искоусьство ('trial, test, experience, mastery, skill'), formed with the suffix -ство from искоусъ ('trial, test, probation') and искоусити ('to test, try', from Proto-Slavic *jьzkusiti; *kusiti is an early borrowing from Gothic kausjan 'to taste, test, try', cognate with English choose). From 'tested mastery and skill', in the 18th century искусство acquired the aesthetic sense 'fine art' (on the model of German Kunst and French art).

исполнить.etymology: Adopted with Old Church Slavonic prefix из- / ис- (from испълнити 'to fill up, accomplish, fulfil'), formed from ис- ('out, completely') + полнить ('to fill', from полный 'full', Proto-Slavic *pъlnъ). Literally 'to fill to the brim, bring to completion'.

использовать.etymology: Biaspectual verb formed from the prefix из- / ис- ('out') + пользовать ('to benefit, use, treat'), derived from польза ('use, benefit, advantage'), which goes back to Old East Slavic польга / польза ('ease, relief, benefit'), from Proto-Slavic *polьga (built on the root *lьg- 'light, easy', as in лёгкий 'light, easy' and льгота 'privilege, relief').

испортить.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the prefix из- / ис- ('out, completely') and портить ('to spoil, ruin, damage'). The base verb портить (attested in Old Russian портити) is derived by Vasmer from портъ ('piece of cut cloth, coarse garment', preserved in портной 'tailor'), originally meaning 'to cut or tear cloth to shreds, mar, ruin'.

history.meaning: cut piece of cloth → to cut up, mar, spoil

исправить.etymology: Borrowed from or modeled on Old Church Slavonic исправити ('to straighten out, set right, correct'), formed from из- / ис- ('out') + правити ('to make straight, direct', from правъ / правый 'straight, right', Proto-Slavic *pravъ).

испытать.etymology: Adopted with Old Church Slavonic prefix из- / ис- (from испытати 'to search out, test thoroughly, experience'), built on ис- ('out, thoroughly') + пытать ('to inquire, test, try', from Proto-Slavic *pytati).

history.meaning: to test, try out; to experience

как-то.etymology: Indefinite adverb formed by attaching the indefinite enclitic particle -то (historically the neuter demonstrative pronoun то 'that') to как ('how', from Proto-Slavic *kako).

history.meaning: somehow, sort of; once, one day

какой-нибудь.etymology: Indefinite pronoun formed from какой ('what kind of, which', from Proto-Slavic *kakъ) and the indefinite enclitic particle -нибудь, historically the univerbated phrase ни будь ('be it whatever it may', from ни + будь, the 2nd sg. imperative of быть 'to be').

каменеть.etymology: Inchoative verb formed with the suffix -еть ('to become...') on the historical consonant stem камен- of камень ('stone', inherited from Old East Slavic камы, genitive камене, from Proto-Slavic *kamy).

history.meaning: stone → to turn to stone, harden like stone

камера.etymology: Borrowed via German Kamera / Kammer and Polish kamera from Latin camera ('vaulted room, arched chamber'), from Ancient Greek καμάρα (kamára, 'anything with an arched cover, vaulted chamber'). In Russian, камера preserves both the older architectural sense ('vaulted cell, prison cell, tire inner tube') and the modern sense ('photographic or video camera', shortened from camera obscura 'dark chamber').

history.meaning: chamber, prison cell; camera (from camera obscura)

кандидат.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via German Kandidat or Polish kandydat from Latin candidātus ('one clothed in white'), derived from candidus ('shining white'). In ancient Rome, office-seekers wore a bleached white toga (toga candida) in the Forum to symbolize purity and integrity.

history.meaning: gleaming white → office-seeker wearing a white toga

кандидатура.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century via German Kandidatur or French candidature, formed with the Medieval Latin office/status suffix -ūra from Latin candidātus ('candidate, office-seeker dressed in a white toga').

капитан.etymology: Borrowed via Polish kapitan from Late Latin capitaneus 'chief, commander', formed on Latin caput 'head'.

капсула.etymology: Borrowed from Latin capsula 'small box or chest', a diminutive of capsa 'box, case for scrolls'. Through French and Italian cousins of capsa, it is a distant doublet of касса and кассета.

капучино.etymology: Borrowed in the late 20th century from Italian cappuccino ('espresso with steamed milk foam'), literally 'Capuchin friar' (from cappuccio 'hood, cowl', because the reddish-brown color of espresso mixed with milk resembled the habit worn by friars of the Capuchin order, and via Viennese Kapuziner coffee).

history.meaning: hood → Capuchin friar → espresso with foamed milk

карандаш.etymology: Borrowed in the sixteenth or seventeenth century from Turkic *qara tas ('black stone, black slate, graphite'), a compound of kara 'black' + tas 'stone', with an intrusive -н- in Russian pronunciation.
карандаш.notes: Writing in pencil takes the instrumental case in Russian: написать карандашом 'to write in pencil'.

карманный.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -ный from карман ('pocket'), borrowed into Russian from Turkic karman ('purse, money-pouch, pocket').

картина.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era (early 18th century) from Italian cartina ('fine paper, small sheet, print'), a diminutive of carta ('paper, card, chart'), from Latin charta and Ancient Greek χάρτης (khártēs, 'sheet of papyrus'). In Russian, картина expanded from an engraving or print on paper to any painting, picture, or motion picture.

картограф.etymology: An international scholarly compound combining карта 'map, chart' + Greek-derived -граф 'one who writes or draws' (from graphein 'to write, draw').

картография.etymology: Borrowed from French cartographie, a scholarly compound formed from Ancient Greek khartes ('sheet of papyrus, map') + -graphia ('drawing, writing').

картошка.etymology: Colloquial and everyday collective/diminutive formed with the suffix -ка from картофель ('potatoes'), borrowed in the 18th century from German Kartoffel (earlier Tartuffel, altered by dissimilation of t-t > k-t from Italian tartufolo 'little truffle', because potato tubers grow underground like truffles).

кастрюля.etymology: Borrowed in the eighteenth century via German Kastrol, a regional variant of Kasserolle, which comes from French casserole 'saucepan' (a diminutive of casse 'pan').

качество.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic качьство ('quality, nature, sort'), formed as a calque of Ancient Greek ποιότης (poiótēs, coined by Plato from ποῖος 'of what kind?', just as Cicero coined Latin quālitās from quālis 'of what kind?'), built from the Slavic interrogative pronoun какъ ('of what kind, how', Russian какой) + the abstract suffix -ьство (-ство), with palatalization of к > ч.

каша.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic каша ('porridge, cooked grain'), from Proto-Slavic *kaša ('porridge, gruel'), cognate with Lithuanian košė ('porridge, mash', from kirti / košti 'to strain, filter').

квадратный.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -ный from квадрат ('square'), borrowed via German Quadrat and Polish kwadrat from Latin quadrātum ('square', from quattuor 'four').

квартира.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via Polish kwatera and German Quartier ('billet, lodging, quarters') from French quartier and Latin quartārius ('fourth part, quarter of a town or camp where soldiers were billeted').

history.meaning: fourth part, district → military quarters, lodging

квота.etymology: Borrowed in the late 19th or early 20th century via German Quote or English quota from Medieval Latin quota (short for quota pars 'how great a part, proportional share'), from Latin quot ('how many').

кино.etymology: Borrowed in the early 20th century from German Kino, a clipping of Kinematograph (compare French cinématographe, coined by the Lumière brothers in the 1890s), from Ancient Greek κίνημα (kínēma, 'movement', from κινέω 'to move') + γράφω (gráphō, 'to write, record').
кино.notes: Indeclinable neuter noun in Russian: **пойти в кино**, **смотреть старое кино**.

кирпич.etymology: Borrowed from Turkic — compare Turkish kerpic, Tatar кирпеч, and Kazakh кірпіш ('sun-dried or fired clay brick') — attested in East Slavic since late medieval building accounts.
кирпич.notes: Stress stays on the ending throughout its declension: кирпич, кирпича, кирпичи, кирпичей.

кислинка.etymology: Formed with the nuance suffix -инка ('a slight touch or trace of a quality') from кислый ('sour, tart', from Proto-Slavic *kyslъ): 'a pleasant touch of tartness or acidity'.

кислить.etymology: Intransitive taste verb formed with -ить from кислый ('sour, tart', from Proto-Slavic *kyslъ), following the productive Russian pattern for flavour nuances (compare горчить 'to taste slightly bitter').

history.meaning: sour → to taste sour, have a tart edge

кислый.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic кислыи ('sour, fermented, acidic'), originally a past active l-participle of киснуть ('to turn sour, ferment', from Proto-Slavic *kysnǫti / *kyslъ).

клад.etymology: Native East Slavic noun built on the root of класть ('to lay, put, stow away'): literally something laid away in a secret spot for safekeeping, hence 'buried treasure, hoard'.

класс.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via German Klasse and French classe from Latin classis ('one of the six property divisions of Roman citizens; fleet, army; school class, rank, category'). In colloquial modern Russian, класс! is also used as an exclamation meaning 'top-class, cool, awesome!'.

кластер.etymology: Borrowed in the second half of the 20th century (first in astronomy, physics, and computing, later in economics and regional policy) from English cluster ('bunch, group of similar things growing or held together'), from Old English clyster ('bunch, cluster').

клиент.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th–19th century via German Klient or French client from Latin cliēns (genitive clientis, 'dependent, follower under the protection of a Roman patrician patron', later 'legal client, customer'), related to clināre ('to lean on') or cluēre ('to hear, obey').

history.meaning: plebeian under a patron's protection; legal client

клоун.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century from English clown ('comic stage rustic, jester, circus clown'), which entered 16th-century English (originally meaning 'clod, boor, country bumpkin') from Low German or Scandinavian (compare Icelandic klunni 'clumsy, boorish fellow' and Low German Klönne).

ключ.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic ключь, from Proto-Slavic *kľučь ('hook, wooden bolt, key'), belonging to an Indo-European family for curved bolts and locks (compare Latin clāvis 'key' and claudō 'to close'). In Russian the same word denotes a door key, a musical clef, and a mechanic's wrench.

клякса.etymology: Borrowed from German Klecks 'blot, splatter of ink', from klecksen 'to blot, splash', adapted into Russian as a feminine -а noun.
клякса.notes: Поставить кляксу means 'to make an ink blot' when writing with a dip nib or fountain pen.

клясться.etymology: Reflexive form of клясть ('to curse, execrate'), inherited from Old East Slavic кляти / клятися (1st sg. кльнуся), from Proto-Slavic *klęti sę ('to swear an oath', literally 'to call down a curse upon oneself if one's word is false').

history.meaning: to bind oneself by a curse → to swear an oath

книга.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic кънига (often plural кънигы 'letters, scroll, book'), from Proto-Slavic *kъniga. Its ultimate pre-Slavic origin is uncertain: Vasmer discusses proposed wanderword routes through Turkic from East Asian or Near Eastern terms for scrolls without a single proven path.

кнопка.etymology: Formed with the Russian suffix -ка from кноп ('small knob, knot, button'), borrowed in the Petrine era from German Knopf or Dutch knoop ('button, knob, knot', cognate with English knob).

history.meaning: push-button; drawing pin, thumbtack; snap fastener

кованый.etymology: Verbal adjective in -ный formed from ковать ('to forge metal, hammer on an anvil, shoe a horse'), inherited from Old East Slavic ковати and Proto-Slavic *kovati ('to strike, forge', cognate with Lithuanian kauti 'to strike, forge' and English hew).

когда-нибудь.etymology: Indefinite temporal adverb formed from когда ('when', from Old East Slavic къгда, Proto-Slavic *kъgda) + the indefinite enclitic particle -нибудь (from ни будь 'be it whenever it may', 2nd sg. imperative of быть 'to be').

history.meaning: whenever it may be → someday, one day, ever

кое-что.etymology: Indefinite pronoun formed from the prefix кое- (historically the neuter singular кое of the archaic interrogative/relative pronoun коий 'which', Proto-Slavic *kъjь) + что ('what', Proto-Slavic *čьto). Typically implies something specific that the speaker knows about but chooses not to name yet ('something, a thing or two').

колпак.etymology: Attested in Old Russian from the 15th century for a tall pointed felt cap or crown; borrowed from Turkic qalpaq ('tall felt or fur cap'; compare Turkish kalpak, Kazakh қалпақ, and Tatar калпак). In modern Russian, колпак denotes a tall chef's toque (поварской колпак), a nightcap, a fool's cap, or a protective glass/lamp dome.

командование.etymology: Verbal noun in -ание from командовать ('to command'), borrowed in the Petrine era via German kommandieren / Polish komenderować from French commander (from Late Latin commandāre 'to entrust, order').

комната.etymology: Borrowed via Polish and Czech komnata from Old High German kemināta, ultimately from Medieval Latin camīnāta ('a room heated by a fireplace', from Latin camīnus 'hearth, stove'). In older Russian architecture it originally meant a warm, heated chamber, before broadening to any indoor room.

history.meaning: room with a hearth or stove

комната.notes: In hotels, an individual guest room is usually called **номер**, while **комната** names a room in a house or flat.

компас.etymology: Borrowed via German Kompass (and Dutch kompas) from Italian compasso 'divider, mariner's compass', derived from Late Latin compassare 'to pace out, measure around' (com- + passus 'step, pace').
компас.notes: Standard everyday Russian stresses the first syllable ком- in компас.

комплимент.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era (early 18th century) via German Kompliment and French compliment from Italian complimento ('act of courtesy, polite expression of praise'), from Spanish cumplimiento ('fulfillment of courtesy'), derived from Latin complēre ('to fill up, complete, fulfill one's polite duty'). In restaurant usage, комплимент от шефа (blended with French/English complimentary) also denotes a free appetizer from the chef.

history.meaning: compliment; complimentary dish from the chef

конверт.etymology: Borrowed from French couvert 'envelope, cover; place setting', originally the past participle of couvrir 'to cover' (from Latin cooperire), with an intrusive н added in Russian pronunciation.

кондитер.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century (earlier кандитор) from German Konditor ('pastry chef, confectioner'), which was adapted in Renaissance German from Latin condītor ('one who seasons, preserves, or pickles food and fruit'), from condīre ('to season, spice, preserve in sugar').

history.meaning: to season, preserve → maker of preserves and sweets

конкурент.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century from German Konkurrent ('competitor, rival'), from Latin concurrēns (genitive concurrentis), present participle of concurrere ('to run together, clash, compete', from com- 'together' + currere 'to run').

контролировать.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century from German kontrollieren (or formed in Russian with -ировать from контроль), from French contrôler ('to verify against a duplicate register, supervise'), from Old French contrerolle ('counter-roll, duplicate ledger used to verify accounts', from contre- + rolle 'scroll, roll').

контроль.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th–19th century via French contrôle (or German Kontrolle) from Old French contrerolle ('duplicate register or roll kept to verify the first'), from Medieval Latin contrārotulus (contrā- 'against' + rotulus 'little wheel, scroll, roll').

history.meaning: duplicate scroll used to audit accounts

конфета.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century (earlier конфекты) via German Konfekt and Polish konfekty from Italian confetto ('candied fruit, sweetmeat, sugar plum'), from Medieval Latin confectum ('something prepared, medicinal preserve or sweetmeat compounded by an apothecary'), neuter past participle of Latin conficere ('to put together, prepare').

концерт.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century via German Konzert and French concert from Italian concerto ('musical performance, harmony, agreement'), derived from concertāre ('to bring into agreement, harmonize; in Latin, to contend, strive together').

кончик.etymology: Diminutive formed with the suffix -чик from конец ('end, tip', with loss of -ец / merger with -чик), inherited from Old East Slavic коньць and Proto-Slavic *konьcь ('end, tip, beginning').

history.meaning: end → very tip, point (кончик носа, кончик пера)

коньяк.etymology: Borrowed from French cognac, named after the town of Cognac in southwestern France (Charente department), where the double-distilled wine brandy has been produced since the 17th century.

history.meaning: town in Charente → brandy from Cognac

копейка.etymology: Shortened from копейная деньга ('lance coin'), introduced during the monetary reform of Elena Glinskaya (mother of Ivan the Terrible) in 1534–1535. The new silver wire coins minted in Moscow depicted the Grand Prince on horseback holding a lance (**копьё**, from Old East Slavic копие, Proto-Slavic *kopьje 'spear, lance'), distinguishing them from older coins showing a saber.

history.meaning: silver coin stamped with a rider holding a lance (копьё)

корешок.etymology: Diminutive in -ок of корень ('root', with stem remodeling корн- → кореш- before -ок), inherited from Old East Slavic корень and Proto-Slavic *korenь ('root'). Extended in bookbinding and stationery to the 'spine' of a book or the 'stub' of a receipt.

history.meaning: root → little root; spine (of a book), ticket stub

корж.etymology: Borrowed in the nineteenth century from Ukrainian корж 'flat dry cake, baked disc of dough', used in Russian baking for each baked pastry layer of a layered cake or tart base.

корица.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic корица (Proto-Slavic *korica), a diminutive of кора 'tree bark' — literally 'little bark', because cinnamon sticks are dried rolls of inner bark.
корица.notes: The Russian adjective коричневый 'brown' comes directly from корица ('cinnamon-coloured')!

корка.etymology: Diminutive in -ка of кора ('tree bark, rind, outer shell'), inherited from Old East Slavic кора and Proto-Slavic *kora ('bark, peel', cognate with Latin corium 'hide, leather, rind').

history.meaning: bark → bread crust, citrus peel, rind

короче.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic короче, the comparative degree of короткий ('short', Old East Slavic коротъкыи, from Proto-Slavic *kortъkъ, comparative *kortje, with East Slavic ч from *tj). In colloquial Russian, короче (short for короче говоря 'speaking more briefly') is ubiquitous as the discourse filler 'in short, anyway, long story short'.

rootFamily.gloss: to stop (Church Slavonic root variant крат-)

коснуться.etymology: Semelfactive perfective verb in -нуть-ся paired with касаться ('to touch'), inherited from Old East Slavic коснути and Proto-Slavic *kosnǫti ('to touch, brush against'), related by o-grade ablaut to чесать ('to scratch, comb', from *česati).

history.meaning: to touch, brush against (takes genitive case)

коснуться.notes: Like *касаться*, *коснуться* governs the genitive case: *коснуться руки* ('to touch a hand').

костюм.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th–19th century from French costume ('customary dress, attire, suit'), which was borrowed from Italian costume ('custom, habit, style of dress'), from Vulgar Latin *cōnsuētūmen (from Classical Latin cōnsuētūdō 'custom, habit').

кофе.etymology: Vasmer traces кофе to English coffee or Dutch koffie, and the wider European word family ultimately to Arabic qahwa. He records the older Russian variants кофей and кофий. The immediate borrowing route is therefore presented as an alternative, not a settled single path.

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: кофе

кофе.notes: In formal Russian, кофе is masculine and indeclinable: чёрный кофе, крепкий кофе. The stress stays on the first syllable.

кошмар.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century from French cauchemar ('nightmare, oppressive dream'), a compound of Old French caucher ('to trample, press down upon', from Latin calcāre 'to tread with the heel') and mare ('night-goblin, incubus', from Germanic/Dutch mare, cognate with the second element of English nightmare).

краситель.etymology: Formed in Russian with the agent/instrument suffix -тель from красить ('to paint, dye, color'), derived from краса ('beauty, bright color', in Old East Slavic especially 'red or bright color', from Proto-Slavic *krasa).

history.meaning: to dye, color → dye, coloring agent

красно-золотой.etymology: Compound colour adjective joining красно- (from красный 'red', originally 'beautiful, bright', Proto-Slavic *krasьnъ) + золотой ('golden', from золото 'gold', Proto-Slavic *zolto).

кредит.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via German Kredit and French crédit from Italian credito ('trust, commercial credit, loan'), from Latin crēditum ('something entrusted, a loan'), neuter past participle of crēdere ('to believe, trust, entrust').

кремовый.etymology: Relational and colour adjective formed with the suffix -овый from крем ('cream, custard, frosting'), borrowed from French crème ('cream', from Late Latin chrisma 'unguent' blended with Gaulish *crama 'cream').

критик.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century via German Kritiker or French critique from Latin criticus, itself from Ancient Greek κριτικός (kritikós, 'able to discern or judge'), derived from κρίνω (krínō, 'to separate, decide, judge').

history.meaning: judge of literature or art, critic

кровь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic кры (accusative кръвь, which replaced the old nominative, just as in любовь and церковь), from Proto-Slavic *kry (genitive *krъve, 'blood'), from Proto-Indo-European *krewh₂- ('raw flesh, clotted blood, gore'; compare Lithuanian kraũjas 'blood', Sanskrit kravíṣ- 'raw flesh', Latin cruor 'blood from a wound' / crūdus 'raw', and English raw).

круассан.etymology: Borrowed from French croissant ('crescent; crescent-shaped flaky pastry'), originally the present participle of croître ('to grow, wax, as the waxing crescent moon'), from Latin crēscere ('to grow'). The Viennese crescent roll (Kipferl) was popularized in Paris in the 19th century as the croissant.

круг.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic кругъ ('circle, disk, wheel'), from Proto-Slavic *krǫgъ ('circle, ring'), cognate with Proto-Germanic *hringaz (the ancestor of English ring and German Ring).

круговой.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -овой from круг ('circle'), from Proto-Slavic *krǫgъ.

кружиться.etymology: Reflexive/intransitive form of кружить ('to circle, whirl, spin'), a denominative verb formed from круг ('circle, wheel, disk', with г > ж before -и-), inherited from Old East Slavic кругъ and Proto-Slavic *krǫgъ ('circle, ring', cognate with Old Norse hringr and English ring).

history.meaning: circle → to move in a circle
to spin, whirl; (голова кружится) to feel dizzy

крупный.etymology: Derived with the adjectival suffix -ный from крупа ('groats, coarse crushed grain', from Old East Slavic крупа and Proto-Slavic *krupa 'coarse grain, lump, hailstone'): originally 'coarse-grained, consisting of large granules' (as in крупная соль 'coarse salt'), then 'large, big, major'.

history.meaning: large, big; coarse (of salt, sand, grain)

крутиться.etymology: Reflexive form in -ся of крутить ('to twist, twirl, turn'), inherited from Old East Slavic крутити and Proto-Slavic *krǫtiti ('to twist, whirl, turn').

history.meaning: to turn → to spin, revolve, turn

крыса.etymology: Attested in Russian from the 16th–17th centuries (earlier крыса / криса; compare dialectal кртыса and Lithuanian kirstùkas 'shrew'). Vasmer connects it with the Proto-Slavic root *krt- / *krys- ('to gnaw, cut, burrow', related to крот 'mole' and Lithuanian kir̃sti 'to cut, bite'). In Russian criminal and prison slang, крыса also means a 'mole, traitor who steals from or informs on his own group'.

крыть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic крыти ('to cover, roof, hide'), from Proto-Slavic *kryti ('to cover'), cognate with Lithuanian krūti / krauti ('to pile up, stack, cover').

крючок.etymology: Diminutive of крюк 'hook' with suffix -ок. Old East Slavic крюкъ was borrowed from Old Norse krokr 'hook, bend' (the same Scandinavian source that gave English crook).

кстати.etymology: Univerbation of the prepositional phrase к стати ('to the proper fit, proportion, or occasion'), from the preposition к ('to') and the dative singular of стать ('form, build, stature, fitting moment', derived from стать 'to stand, become', Proto-Slavic *statь). From meaning 'fittingly, at an opportune moment' (это очень кстати), it also grammaticalized into the discourse marker 'by the way, speaking of which'.

history.meaning: to the proper fit or occasion, opportunely

кулинарный.etymology: Adjective formed with the suffix -ный from кулинар / кулинария ('culinary art, cookery'), borrowed in the 19th century via German kulinarisch / French culinaire from Latin culīnārius ('pertaining to the kitchen'), from culīna ('kitchen').

курица.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic курица ('hen, chicken'), formed with the feminine suffix -ица from куръ ('rooster, cock', preserved in курятник 'henhouse' and the proverb попасть как кур во щи), from Proto-Slavic *kurъ ('rooster'), an onomatopoeic formation imitating the bird's crowing.

кухня.etymology: Vasmer records кухня from 1717, with поварня used earlier. He traces the borrowing through Polish and Czech to an Old High German word for kitchen, ultimately from Latin coquina. The Russian word belongs to a much-travelled European kitchen-word family.

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: кухня

кухонный.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -ный from кухня ('kitchen', inserting a fleeting о inside the stem кухн-), which entered Russian in the early eighteenth century via Polish kuchnia and Old High German kuchina from Late Latin coquīna ('kitchen').

кушать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic кушати / покушати ('to taste, try, test, experience'), from Proto-Slavic *kušati (iterative of *kusiti 'to taste, try', an early borrowing from Gothic kausjan 'to taste, test', from the same root as вкус 'taste' and искусство). From 'tasting or sampling food and drink', кушать became a polite or deferential verb for 'to eat' (traditionally used when inviting guests to eat — Кушайте, пожалуйста! — or when speaking to children).

history.meaning: to eat (polite invitation or with children)

кушать.notes: In careful standard Russian, adults usually say **я ем** (from **есть**) about themselves rather than *я кушаю*, reserving **кушать** for polite invitations (**Кушать подано!**, **Кушайте!**) and children.

лаборатория.etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin laboratorium 'workshop, place of scientific work', built on Latin laborare 'to work, take pains' from labor 'toil, effort'.

лезть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic лѣзти (present лѣзу), from Proto-Slavic *lězti ('to climb, crawl, creep'), cognate with Latvian lēzēt ('to slide, creep') and Old Prussian līse ('crawls'). In colloquial Russian, лезть also means 'to barge in, meddle, stick one's nose into' (не лезь не в своё дело).

history.meaning: to climb, reach into; to intrude, meddle

лейтенант.etymology: Borrowed in the 17th–18th century via German Leutnant from French lieutenant ('deputy, officer acting in place of a superior'), a compound of lieu ('place', from Latin locus) + tenant ('holding', present participle of tenir 'to hold', from Latin tenēre), literally 'place-holder'.

лепесток.etymology: Diminutive in -ок of dialectal and older Russian лепест ('leaf, petal, thin flap'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *lepestъ ('leaf, petal, flake'), built on an expressive Balto-Slavic root *lep- ('to flutter, peel, leaf'; compare лист and Lithuanian lapas 'leaf').

history.meaning: leaf, flap → flower petal; thin flake (of almonds or pastry)

лестница.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic лѣствица / лѣстница, from Proto-Slavic *lěstvica, built on the verb лезть (*lězti, 'to climb'). Literally 'something for climbing'; the middle т is silent in modern pronunciation ('lesnitsa').

лечить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic лѣчити ('to heal, cure, treat'), from Proto-Slavic *lěčiti, a denominative verb from *lěkъ ('medicine, remedy, healing charm'; preserved in лекарство 'medicine', Polish lek 'medicine', and Czech lék). Most etymologists (including Vasmer) trace *lěkъ to an early borrowing from Gothic lēkeis ('physician, healer'; compare Old English lǣċe 'physician', archaic English leech). In modern Russian slang, лечить кого-то also means 'to lecture, feed tall tales, try to talk someone into something'.

history.meaning: to treat medically; (slang) to lecture, spin a yarn

листать.etymology: Denominative verb formed in Russian from лист ('leaf of a tree; sheet or page of paper', inherited from Old East Slavic листъ and Proto-Slavic *listъ).

history.meaning: sheet, page → to leaf through, turn pages

листочек.etymology: Double diminutive formed with -ек from листок ('small leaf; sheet of paper', with к → ч before -ек), itself the diminutive in -ок of лист ('leaf; sheet of paper', from Old East Slavic листъ and Proto-Slavic *listъ).

history.meaning: leaf, sheet → small leaf; slip of paper

лицевой.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -евой from лицо ('face; front or right side of cloth, a building, or a page'), inherited from Old East Slavic лице and Proto-Slavic *lice ('face, cheek, outward appearance').

history.meaning: face, front → front, facing, obverse (лицевая сторона 'front side')

лично.etymology: Adverbial form in -о of личный ('personal'), derived from лицо ('face, person', from Old East Slavic лице and Proto-Slavic *lice).

личный.etymology: Derived from лицо ('face; person, individual', Old East Slavic лице, Proto-Slavic *lice) with palatalization of ц > ч before the adjectival suffix -ный. As лицо developed the legal and grammatical sense 'person, individual' (influenced by Old Church Slavonic translating Greek πρόσωπον), личный came to mean 'personal, private, individual'.

ловить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic ловити ('to hunt, catch, fish'), from Proto-Slavic *loviti, a denominative verb from *lovъ ('hunting, catch, prey').

ложь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic лъжь ('lie, falsehood'), from Proto-Slavic *lъžь, a feminine i-stem noun derived from the root of лгать ('to lie', Old East Slavic лъгати, Proto-Slavic *lъgati), from Proto-Indo-European *lewgʰ- ('to tell a lie'; exact cognate with German Lüge and English lie).

лом.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic ломъ ('breaking, windfall timber, pry bar, scrap'), a deverbal o-grade noun from ломить / ломать ('to break, fracture'), from Proto-Slavic *lomъ. As a tool, a лом is a heavy iron bar for breaking ice, stone, or prying.

history.meaning: breaking; heavy pry bar; broken pieces

луч.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic лучь ('ray of light, beam; resinous pine torch'), from Proto-Slavic *lučь, continuing the Proto-Indo-European root *lewk- ('bright, light, shine'), cognate with Latin lūx ('light') and English light.

льстить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic льстити and Old Church Slavonic льстити ('to deceive, cajole, flatter'), derived from лесть ('flattery; in older Slavic, guile or deceit'), from Proto-Slavic *lьstь, an early borrowing from Proto-Germanic *listiz ('cunning, skill, craft', compare German List).

любовница.etymology: Feminine counterpart of любовник ('lover'), formed with the feminine agent suffix -ница from любовный ('amorous, of love'), derived from любовь ('love', Old East Slavic любы / любовь, Proto-Slavic *ľuby).

любовь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic любы (accusative любовь, which replaced the old nominative, just as in кровь and морковь), from Proto-Slavic *ľuby (genitive *ľubъve, 'love, affection'), from Proto-Indo-European *lewbʰ- ('to care, desire, love'; cognate with English love, German Liebe, and Sanskrit lúbhyati 'desires').
любовь.notes: When used as a common noun ('love'), the vowel **о** is fleeting in oblique cases (**любви́**, **любо́вью**); in the female given name **Любо́вь**, the **о** is retained throughout (**у Любо́ви**).

любой.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic любыи ('dear, pleasing, whichever one pleases'), from Proto-Slavic *ľubъ ('dear, beloved', cognate with любить 'to love' and English lief / love). From phrases like на любой выбор ('whichever pleases you') it grammaticalized into the determiner 'any'.

м.etymology: The fourteenth letter of the Russian Cyrillic alphabet (named эм in modern Russian, and мыслѣте 'think!' in the traditional Old Church Slavonic acrostic alphabet), adapted from the Greek letter mu (Μ, μ), ultimately from Phoenician mem ('water').

history.meaning: the letter M; standard abbreviation for метр ('metre') or минута

майор.etymology: Borrowed in the 17th century via German Major (and Polish major) from Spanish mayor / French major, shortened from sergeant-major, ultimately from Latin maior ('greater, senior', comparative of magnus 'great').

мало.etymology: Adverb and quantifier formed from the neuter short form of малый ('small, little'), inherited from Old East Slavic мало / малъ, from Proto-Slavic *malъ ('small, little'). Vasmer compares Gothic smals ('small'), Ancient Greek μῆλον ('small cattle, sheep'), and Latin malus.

малыш.etymology: Formed in Russian with the expressive noun suffix -ыш from малый ('small, little'), inherited from Old East Slavic малъ and Proto-Slavic *malъ ('small').

марка.etymology: Borrowed via German Marke 'mark, token, stamp' from French marque, of Germanic origin (akin to mark 'sign, boundary'). Used in Russian both for a postage stamp (почтовая марка) and for a brand or make.

маршрут.etymology: Borrowed in the eighteenth century from German Marschroute ('line of march, planned itinerary'), a compound of Marsch ('march') + Route ('road, route'), both originally from French.
маршрут.notes: Everyday Russian uses маршрут for bus and tram lines as well as walking or travel itineraries.

масло.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic масло ('butter, oil'), from Proto-Slavic *maslo (< *maz-slo), built from мазать ('to spread, smear, anoint') plus suffix *-slo: literally 'something spread on bread'.

матч.etymology: Borrowed in the late 19th century from English match ('sports contest, game between two matched sides'), from Middle English macche ('equal, opponent, counterpart, contest'), from Old English ġemæcca ('mate, companion, equal').

мать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic мати (accusative матерь, which gave the modern nominative мать, while the ancient consonant stem -ер- is preserved in all oblique cases: матери, матерью, матерей), from Proto-Slavic *mati (genitive *matere), from Proto-Indo-European *méh₂tēr ('mother'; compare Sanskrit mātṛ́, Ancient Greek μήτηρ, Latin māter, Lithuanian mótė, German Mutter, and English mother).

машинка.etymology: Diminutive of машина ('machine, engine; car'), formed with the suffix -ка. Base noun машина was borrowed in the Petrine era via German Maschine / French machine from Latin māchina ('device, engine, contrivance'), from Doric Greek μαχανά (mākhaná, Attic μηχανή mēkhanḗ). While машина in everyday Russian came to mean a full-sized 'car, automobile', the diminutive машинка denotes either a 'toy car' or a small household/office appliance (стиральная машинка 'washing machine', пишущая машинка 'typewriter', машинка для стрижки 'hair clippers').

медаль.etymology: Borrowed via French medaille from Italian medaglia 'coin, medallion', going back to Late Latin medalia 'small coin worth half a denarius' (related to Latin medius 'middle, half').

мелисса.etymology: Borrowed via botanical Latin melissa from Ancient Greek μέλισσα (mélissa 'honeybee', derived from μέλι 'honey'), because the fragrant lemon-scented herb attracts bees (hence its traditional name 'bee balm' or 'lemon balm').

менять.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic мѣняти ('to exchange, swap, change'), from Proto-Slavic *měňati, built on *měna ('exchange, barter, change'), from Proto-Indo-European *mey- ('to change, exchange', cognate with Latin mūnus / commūnis and Latvian mainīt 'to exchange').

металлический.etymology: Adjective formed with the suffix -ический from металл ('metal'), borrowed via German Metall / French métal from Latin metallum and Ancient Greek μέταλλον ('mine, quarry; mineral, metal').

мечеть.etymology: Attested in Old Russian chronicles and travel accounts from the 14th–15th centuries (as мечеть / мизгить), borrowed via Volga Bulgar or Kipchak Turkic mäčät / mäčit from Arabic مَسْجِد (masjid, 'mosque', literally 'place of prostration in prayer', from sajada 'to bow down, prostrate oneself'; the same Arabic word gave Spanish mezquita and English mosque).

мечтать.etymology: Derived from мечта ('daydream, cherished wish, vision'), adopted via Old Church Slavonic мьчьта ('phantasm, vision, imagination'), from Proto-Slavic *mьčьta, built on the root *mьk- / *mьg- ('to flicker, gleam, flash before the eyes'; compare мигать 'to blink, twinkle').

мешочек.etymology: Double diminutive formed with -ек from мешок ('bag, sack', with к → ч before -ек), itself a derivative in -ок of Old East Slavic мѣхъ ('animal skin, wineskin, fur bag', from Proto-Slavic *měxъ).

history.meaning: bag, sack → small pouch, little bag

миллион.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via French million or German Million from Italian milione (attested in the 13th–14th centuries, famously in Marco Polo's Il Milione), an augmentative of mille ('thousand', from Latin mīlle), literally 'a great thousand' (1,000 × 1,000).

миндаль.etymology: Entered Russian via Old Church Slavonic мигдалъ and Polish migdal from Latin amygdalus and Ancient Greek amygdale 'almond', with the consonant cluster reshaping smoothly to миндаль in East Slavic.

cognates.meaning: almond (via Old French almande from the same Latin word)

миндаль.notes: Used as a collective masculine singular noun in culinary Russian: жареный миндаль 'roasted almonds'.

мир.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic миръ ('peace, concord; village community; the universe, world'), from Proto-Slavic *mirъ ('peace, world order'), cognate with Lithuanian mieras ('peace') and Sanskrit mitrá ('friend, alliance'). In pre-1918 orthography the two senses were artificially distinguished as миръ ('peace') and міръ ('world, community'), though both descend from the same Slavic word.
мир.notes: The proverb *Мир тесен* literally means 'The world is cramped/narrow' — i.e., 'It's a small world!'.

молодец.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic молодьць ('young man, brave warrior, gallant youth'), formed from молодъ / молодой ('young', displaying East Slavic pleophony -оло- from Proto-Slavic *moldъ) + the masculine noun suffix -ец. In folk poetry, добрый молодец meant a 'strapping, valiant youth', which generalized into an exclamation of praise ('well done! good job!').

молоко.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic молоко (showing East Slavic pleophony -оло-; compare Old Church Slavonic млѣко and Polish mleko), from Proto-Slavic *melko. Vasmer compares Proto-Germanic *meluk- (English milk, German Milch), noting that scholars debate whether Slavic borrowed the word early from Germanic or shared an older western Indo-European root.

молоток.etymology: Diminutive in -ок of молот ('heavy sledgehammer'), inherited from Old East Slavic молотъ (with East Slavic pleophony -оло-) and Proto-Slavic *moltъ ('hammer, mallet'), derived from the same root as молоть ('to grind, crush', Proto-Indo-European *melh₂-, cognate with Latin malleus 'hammer, mallet'). Eventually молоток became the everyday Russian word for a hand hammer.

молотый.etymology: Past passive participle of молоть ('to grind, mill'), inherited from Old East Slavic молоти (with regular East Slavic pleophony -оло-) and Proto-Slavic *melti ('to grind', from Proto-Indo-European *melh₂-, cognate with Latin molere and English mill / meal).

history.meaning: to grind → ground, finely milled (молотый кофе 'ground coffee')

момент.etymology: Borrowed in the early 18th century via German Moment or French moment from Latin mōmentum ('movement, impulse, brief particle of time', contracted from *movimentum), derived from movēre ('to move').

монастырь.etymology: Borrowed in the Old East Slavic period (attested from the 11th century as манастырь / монастырь) from Byzantine Greek μοναστήριον (monastḗrion, 'hermitage, monastery'), from μοναστήρ / μοναχός (monakhós, 'monk, solitary'), derived from μόνος (mónos, 'alone, solitary').

монета.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via Polish moneta from Latin moneta 'mint; coined money', named after the temple of Juno Moneta on the Capitoline Hill in Rome, beside which silver coins were struck.

history.meaning: epithet of Juno; the Roman mint; coin

cognates.meaning: place where coins are struck (early Germanic loan from Latin moneta)

морщиться.etymology: Reflexive form in -ся of морщить ('to wrinkle, crease, pucker'), derived from морщина / морск ('wrinkle, fold, pucker', from Proto-Slavic *morščiti).

history.meaning: to wrinkle → to wince, pucker up one's face (e.g. from sourness)

мост.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic мостъ ('bridge; timber-paved street'), from Proto-Slavic *mostъ. Vasmer connects it most plausibly with метать ('to throw, lay across': logs laid across water or mud), an older sense still visible in мостовая ('cobblestone or paved roadway').

муж.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic мужь (and Old Church Slavonic мѫжь 'man, husband'), from Proto-Slavic *mǫžь ('man, male, husband'), from Proto-Indo-European *mon-gʷ-yo- / *man-u- ('man'; compare Sanskrit mányate / mánu-, German Mann, and English man).

мужик.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic мужикъ (attested from the 13th–14th centuries), formed with the diminutive/expressive suffix -ик from мужь / муж ('man, husband', Proto-Slavic *mǫžь). Historically denoting a commoner or peasant man as opposed to a nobleman, in modern colloquial Russian мужик means 'guy, bloke' or 'a tough, real man'.

мучить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic мучити ('to torment, torture'), a denominative verb from мука ('torment, torture, agony'; note stress **му́ка**, distinct from **мука́** 'flour', though both share the same root!), from Proto-Slavic *mǫka ('torment; flour', originally 'crushing, kneading, pressing', from PIE *menk- 'to knead, crush', cognate with Lithuanian mìnkyti 'to knead dough').

мы.etymology: An inherited Slavic first-person plural pronoun, recorded in Old Church Slavonic as мы. Vasmer compares Baltic relatives, including Lithuanian mes. He discusses possible reshaping of the pronoun by analogy with other grammatical forms; that detail is a proposed historical explanation rather than a simple borrowing story.

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: мы

мэр.etymology: Borrowed from French maire ('mayor, head of a municipality'), from Latin māior ('greater, elder, superior', comparative of magnus 'great').

мягко.etymology: Adverbial form in -о of мягкий ('soft, gentle'), from Old East Slavic мягъко and Proto-Slavic *mękъko (with dissimilation of *k-k to гк).
мягко.notes: Pronounced [мя́хка], with г devoicing and spirantizing to [х] before к.

мякиш.etymology: Formed with the noun suffix -иш from мягкий (historically мякъкыи 'soft', from Proto-Slavic *mękъkъ): literally 'the soft inner part' of a loaf of bread or cake, as opposed to the crust (корка).

history.meaning: soft → soft inside crumb of baked bread or cake

мясной.etymology: Relational adjective inherited from Old East Slavic мясьныи, formed with the suffix -ной from мясо ('meat, flesh'), from Proto-Slavic *męso (cognate with Lithuanian mėsà, Sanskrit māṃsá-, and Gothic mimz).

мясо.etymology: An inherited Slavic word for meat or flesh. Vasmer records it across the Slavic languages and compares Baltic and Indo-Iranian relatives. It belongs to an older inherited word family rather than being a recent Russian borrowing.

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: мясо

мясо.notes:
- Common collocations: *жареное мясо* (fried meat), *куриное мясо* (chicken meat).
- Genitive plural *мяс* is rare; the word is mostly used in the singular.

мята.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *męta, an early borrowing from Latin menta 'mint' (with nasal *ę regularly yielding Russian я), which comes from Ancient Greek minthe.

cognates.meaning: aromatic herb (early borrowing from Latin menta)

мята.notes: Comparing Polish mięta (preserving the nasal vowel) with Russian мята nicely illustrates the regular Slavic sound law *ę -> я.

навес.etymology: Deverbal noun from навесить ('to hang or suspend overhead'), formed from prefix на- ('over, above') + весить ('to hang', from Proto-Slavic *věsiti). Denotes a roofed shelter, awning, or canopy projecting over an entrance or courtyard.

history.meaning: to hang overhead → overhanging roof, canopy

навести.etymology: Perfective verb inherited from Old East Slavic навести (1st sg. наведу), formed from the prefix на- ('onto, upon') and вести ('to lead, conduct', from Proto-Slavic *vesti). Used both literally ('to direct, aim, lead onto; to build a bridge across') and in common idioms such as навести порядок ('to put in order, tidy up') and навести справки ('to make inquiries').

history.meaning: to direct, aim; to establish (навести порядок)

наглый.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic наглыи ('sudden, headlong, impetuous'), from Proto-Slavic *naglъ ('sudden, abrupt, rash', compare Polish nagły 'sudden, abrupt, urgent' and Czech náhlý 'sudden'). In Russian, the meaning shifted from acting with 'headlong abruptness' (preserved in нагрянуть) to acting with 'brazen, shameless impudence'.

надежда.etymology: Adopted from Old Church Slavonic надежда ('hope, reliance'), showing the characteristic South Slavic reflex -жд- from Proto-Slavic *dj (compare the native East Slavic root in надёжный 'reliable'), formed from на- ('upon') + *děti ('to put, place'): literally 'putting one's trust upon something'.

надеть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic надѣти, from Proto-Slavic *naděti ('to put on, place upon'), formed from the prefix *na- ('on, onto') and *děti ('to put, place', Russian деть, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁- 'to put, do').
надеть.notes: Standard Russian distinguishes **надеть** ('to put an item of clothing on oneself': *надеть пальто, надеть очки*) from **одеть** ('to dress a person': *одеть ребёнка*).

надоесть.etymology: Formed from the prefix над- / надо- ('over, upon, to excess') and есть ('to eat', Old East Slavic ѣсти, Proto-Slavic *ěsti, from PIE *h₁ed-). Literally 'to eat away at someone, gnaw at someone to excess', whence 'to bore to death, make someone sick and tired of something' (мне это надоело).

history.meaning: to gnaw at, eat away at
to bore, get on someone's nerves, make sick and tired of (+ dat.)

надёжность.etymology: Abstract noun formed with the suffix -ость from надёжный ('reliable, trustworthy, sturdy'), the native East Slavic counterpart (with ж from *dj and ё before a hard consonant) of Church Slavonic надежда ('hope, reliance', from на- + деть 'to place trust upon').

назвать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic назьвати ('to call by name, summon'), formed from the prefix на- and звать ('to call', Old East Slavic зъвати, Proto-Slavic *zъvati, cognate with Sanskrit hváyati 'calls, invokes').

назначить.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the prefix на- and значить ('to mark, signify, mean'), derived from знак ('sign, mark', from Proto-Slavic *znakъ, built on *znati 'to know'). Literally, 'to put a mark on, designate for a role or time', whence 'to appoint (to a post), set (a date/meeting), or prescribe (treatment)'.

history.meaning: to appoint, designate, set (a time), prescribe

называться.etymology: Imperfective reflexive/passive verb formed from называть ('to call, name', imperfective of назвать, with lengthened root vowel -ы- from Proto-Slavic *nazyvati, built on *zъvati 'to call'). Means 'to be called, have the name/title of'.

rootFamily.gloss: name, title (of an object, book, restaurant)

найтись.etymology: Perfective reflexive/passive form of найти ('to find', literally 'to come upon by walking', from на- 'onto, upon' + йти / идти 'to go', Old East Slavic наити, Proto-Slavic *najьti). With -сь, найтись means 'to be found, turn up' (and figuratively 'to find the right words, not be at a loss').

rootFamily.gloss: to be located; to be found (impf.)

наказать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic наказати ('to instruct, admonish, teach a lesson'), formed from the prefix на- and казати ('to show, point out, speak', Proto-Slavic *kazati). Up to the 18th century, наказать meant 'to instruct, give orders' (preserved in наказ 'mandate, instruction to a deputy'); from 'teaching someone a stern lesson', it shifted in modern Russian to 'to punish'.

наклонить.etymology: Formed with the prefix на- ('downward, toward') + клонить ('to incline, bend, tilt'), inherited from Old East Slavic клонити and Proto-Slavic *kloniti.

наклониться.etymology: Reflexive form in -ся of наклонить ('to tilt, bend down'), formed with prefix на- ('onto, downward') + клонить ('to incline, bend, bow', from Proto-Slavic *kloniti).

history.meaning: to tilt → to lean down, bend over

нанести.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic нанести ('to bring upon, lay on'), formed from prefix на- ('onto, upon a surface') + нести ('to carry, bring', from Proto-Slavic *nesti). Used for brushing on glaze/paint, plotting marks on a map, or paying a visit.

history.meaning: to apply, brush on (glaze, paint), mark (on a map)

напиток.etymology: Inherited from East Slavic напитокъ, formed with the noun suffix -ок from напить / напиться ('to drink one's fill', passive participle напитый), built from the prefix на- and пить ('to drink', Proto-Slavic *piti).

например.etymology: Univerbation of the prepositional phrase на пример ('for an example, after the model of'), formed from the preposition на ('for, onto') + пример ('example, model'), which is derived from примерить ('to try on, measure against', from при- + мерить 'to measure', built on мера 'measure', Proto-Slavic *měra).

напугать.etymology: Perfective counterpart of пугать ('to scare, frighten'), formed with the prefix на- and the expressive East Slavic verb пугать (compare dialectal пуга 'whip; owl' and Ukrainian пугач 'eagle owl', from an onomatopoeic cry *pug- used to startle birds or animals).

нарезать.etymology: Formed from the cumulative prefix на- ('in a quantity, into pieces') and резать ('to cut, slice'), inherited from Old East Slavic рѣзати and Proto-Slavic *rězati ('to cut, carve', cognate with Lithuanian rė́žti 'to cut, incise'). Note that stress distinguishes aspect: perfective **наре́зать** ('to slice up') vs. imperfective **нареза́ть**.

народ.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic народъ ('people, multitude, lineage'), from Proto-Slavic *narodъ, a deverbal noun formed from *naroditi ('to give birth to in numbers, beget, produce'), from *na- + *roditi ('to give birth', Russian родить). Literally, 'that which has been born or grown up together, a generation or people'.

народный.etymology: Relational adjective inherited from Old East Slavic народьныи, formed from народ ('people, nation', from Proto-Slavic *narodъ) + the adjectival suffix -ный.

нарушение.etymology: Verbal noun formed from нарушить ('to break, violate, disturb'), built from на- + рушить ('to break down, tear down, shatter', from Proto-Slavic *rušiti). Just as English speaks of 'breaking' a law or rule, Russian uses нарушить / нарушение for the 'breach or violation' of a rule, law, or order.

history.meaning: to break (a rule/peace) → violation, breach, infringement

насквозь.etymology: Adverb formed in Russian from prefix на- + сквозь ('through, right through'), inherited from Old East Slavic сквозѣ and Proto-Slavic *skvozě ('through an opening or gap').

history.meaning: right through, all the way through

настроение.etymology: Verbal noun from настроить ('to tune a musical instrument; to attune, put in a frame of mind'), built from на- + строить ('to arrange, order, build', from Proto-Slavic *strojiti). Just as German Stimmung ('mood') comes from stimmen ('to tune an instrument'), Russian настроение shifted from 'the tuning of strings' to a person's emotional 'mood, frame of mind'.

history.meaning: tuning of a musical instrument → emotional attunement, mood

наступить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic наступити ('to step upon, advance; to come upon'), formed from the prefix на- ('on, onto') and ступить ('to step, tread', from Proto-Slavic *stǫpiti). Has two primary uses in modern Russian: physical ('to step on something', наступить на ногу) and temporal ('to come, set in, arrive', of seasons, times of day, or events: наступила зима).

history.meaning: to step on; to set in
to step on (+ на); to come, arrive (of time/events)

натворить.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the cumulative prefix на- ('in a quantity') and творить ('to create, make, do'), inherited from Old East Slavic творити and Proto-Slavic *tvoriti ('to form, shape, make', related to тварь 'creature'). In modern colloquial Russian, натворить specialized in a negative or ironic sense: 'to do something bad, cause a mess or trouble' (Что ты натворил? 'What have you done?!').

history.meaning: to do/make (especially mischief, trouble, or a mess)

научить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic научити, formed from the perfective prefix на- and учить ('to teach', from Proto-Slavic *učiti, causative of the PIE root *h₁ewk- 'to become accustomed, learn').

history.meaning: to teach (someone: acc. + чему: dat. or infinitive)

научиться.etymology: Perfective reflexive verb formed by adding -ся ('oneself') to научить ('to teach'), from Old East Slavic научити, built from на- + учить ('to teach', Proto-Slavic *učiti, causative of the PIE root *h₁ewk- 'to become accustomed'). Literally, 'to teach oneself, acquire a skill'.

находчивый.etymology: Formed with the adjectival suffix -чивый from находить / находка ('to find, hit upon a solution / a clever find'), built on на- ('upon') + ходить ('to go, walk'): 'quick at finding a solution, resourceful'.

history.meaning: to find / a find → resourceful, quick-witted

начальник.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic начальникъ (and Old Church Slavonic начѧльникъ 'founder, leader, chief'), formed from начало ('beginning, command, authority', from начать 'to begin', Proto-Slavic *načęti) + the agent suffix -ник.

history.stage: Old Church Slavonic / Old East Slavic

начаться.etymology: Perfective intransitive/reflexive verb formed by adding -ся to начать ('to begin, start'), inherited from Old East Slavic начати, from Proto-Slavic *načęti ('to begin', from *na- + *čęti, related to конец 'end').

не.etymology: The negative particle не is inherited from older Slavic, rather than being a recent borrowing. Vasmer compares negative forms across the Indo-European languages, including Latin ne- and Baltic ne. The Russian particle also appears in word formation, but a prefixed word may develop a meaning of its own.

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: не

небольшой.etymology: Formed in Russian by prefixing negative не- ('not, un-') to большой ('big, large', from Old East Slavic большии 'bigger, greater'), yielding a litotes meaning 'small, modest-sized'.

неважно.etymology: Formed with negative не- ('not') + важно ('importantly; it is important'), from важный ('weighty, important', borrowed via Polish ważny from Old High German wāga 'weight, scales').

history.meaning: not important → never mind, it does not matter; (colloquial) poorly

невероятно.etymology: Adverbial and predicate form in -о of невероятный ('incredible, improbable'), formed with negative не- + вероятный ('probable, likely', literally 'capable of being taken on trust', a Church Slavonic-modelled compound of вера 'faith, belief' + яти 'to take', calquing German wahrscheinlich / Latin vērīsimilis).

невозможно.etymology: Adverb and impersonal predicate formed from невозможный ('impossible'), built with the negative prefix не- on возможный ('possible'), which derives from Old Church Slavonic възмощи / возмочь ('to be able, have the power to', from въз- + мощи / мочь 'to be able, can', Proto-Slavic *moťi).

невыезд.etymology: Formed with the negative prefix не- ('non-') from выезд ('departure, exit by vehicle, trip out'), a deverbal noun from выехать ('to drive out, depart', from вы- + ехать 'to go by vehicle', Proto-Slavic *ěxati). Used almost exclusively in the legal formula **подписка о невыезде** ('signed undertaking not to leave town pending trial or investigation').

незабываемый.etymology: Formed with negative prefix не- ('un-') + забываемый (present passive participle of забывать 'to forget', built on за- + бывать / быть 'to be'). Literally 'not able to be forgotten, unforgettable'.

незнакомец.etymology: Built transparently from не- 'un-, not' + знакомец 'acquaintance' (from знакомый 'familiar, known' + person suffix -ец, ultimately from знать 'to know').

немедленно.etymology: Adverb formed from the adjective немедленный ('immediate, unhesitating'), built with the negative prefix не- on медленный ('slow'), historically a participle related to медлить ('to delay, tarry', from Proto-Slavic *mьdьlъ 'slow, sluggish').

немецкий.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic нѣмьчьскыи ('foreign, Western European, German'), formed from нѣмьць / немец ('German; in medieval Rus', any foreigner speaking an unintelligible Western tongue'), derived with the suffix *-ьcь from нѣмъ / немой ('mute, dumb, unable to speak intelligibly', Proto-Slavic *němъ). Early Slavs contrasted themselves — словене, 'people of the intelligible word (слово)' — with their western neighbors, *němьci ('those who cannot speak [our language]').

history.meaning: mute → speaker of an unintelligible tongue, Germanic neighbor

ненавидеть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic ненавидѣти (and Old Church Slavonic ненавидѣти 'to hate'), from Proto-Slavic *nenaviděti, formed with the negative prefix *ne- on *naviděti ('to look gladly upon, favor'), itself from *na- ('upon') + *viděti ('to see, look at', Russian видеть). Literally, 'not to bear looking at someone' (compare Latin invidia 'envy', from in- + vidēre).

history.meaning: to be unable to look upon → to hate

неправда.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic неправьда ('injustice, falsehood, untruth'), formed with the negative prefix не- and правда ('truth, justice', derived from правый 'right, true, straight', Proto-Slavic *pravьda).

неправильно.etymology: Adverb formed with the negative prefix не- from правильно ('correctly, rightly'), derived from правильный ('correct, right') and правило ('rule'), ultimately from правый ('straight, right', Proto-Slavic *pravъ).

неправый.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic неправыи ('unjust, crooked, wrong'), formed with the negative prefix не- and правый ('right, straight, just', from Proto-Slavic *pravъ). In modern Russian, it is used almost exclusively in the short predicate forms **неправ / неправа / неправы** ('wrong, mistaken': ты неправ 'you are wrong').

нервничать.etymology: Formed in 19th-century Russian with the colloquial behavioral verb suffix -ничать from нервный ('nervous'), itself derived from нерв ('nerve'), borrowed via German Nerv / French nerf from Latin nervus ('sinew, tendon, nerve').

history.meaning: nervous → to act nervously, fret, worry

morphemes.meaning: to behave in a certain manner

нечего.etymology: Negative predicative pronoun (stressed on the first syllable: **не́чего**, literally 'there is nothing [to do]') inherited from Old East Slavic нечего, contracted from *не есть чего ('there is not of what', where не is fused with the lost present copula *е / есть and чего is the genitive of что 'what', Proto-Slavic *čьto). Distinct in stress and meaning from **нечего́ / ничего́** ('nothing').

history.meaning: there is nothing (to); no point in (+ infinitive)

нечего.notes: Followed by an infinitive (with an optional dative subject): **Мне не́чего сказать** ('I have nothing to say'), **Не́чего делать** ('There's nothing to do').

нигде.etymology: Negative locative adverb inherited from Old East Slavic никъдѣ, formed from the negative prefix ни- and где ('where', Old East Slavic къдѣ, from Proto-Slavic *kъde).

низ.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic низъ ('down, bottom, low ground'), from Proto-Slavic *nizъ ('bottom, downward'), continuing a Proto-Indo-European spatial stem *ni- ('down, below', cognate with English beneath and German nieder).

никак.etymology: Negative adverb formed from the negative prefix ни- and как ('how', from Old East Slavic како, Proto-Slavic *kako).

history.meaning: in no way, by no means, not at all

никуда.etymology: Negative directional adverb formed from the negative prefix ни- and куда ('where to, whither', from Old East Slavic кудѣ / куда, Proto-Slavic *kǫdě).
никуда.notes: Russian distinguishes location (**нигде** 'nowhere, in no place') from direction of motion (**никуда** 'to nowhere': *я никуда не пойду*).

ниша.etymology: Borrowed as an architectural term from French niche ('wall recess'), from Old French nichier 'to make a nest', going back to Latin nidus 'nest' (distant Indo-European cousin of Russian гнездо and English nest).

новый.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic новъ, from Proto-Slavic *novъ, from Proto-Indo-European *néwos ('new'), cognate with English new, German neu, French neuf/nouveau, Latin novus, and Ancient Greek νέος.

нож.etymology: Нож is an inherited Slavic word, recorded as ножь in Old Russian and Old Church Slavonic. Vasmer connects its historical root with заноза, вонзить and пронзить: words involving a splinter, piercing or thrusting into something. That connection gives the knife word a history associated with a pointed or piercing object.

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: нож

ножка.etymology: Diminutive in -ка of нога ('foot, leg', with regular velar palatalization г → ж before -к-), inherited from Old East Slavic ножька and Proto-Slavic *nožьka. Used both for a small foot and for the supporting leg or stem of a chair, table, or glass.

history.meaning: foot, leg → little foot; furniture leg

номер.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era (via German Nummer or Dutch nummer) from Latin numerus / Italian numero ('number'). In 19th-century Russian inns and hotels, номер ('a numbered room') became the standard everyday word for a hotel room.

нормально.etymology: Adverbial and predicate form in -о of нормальный ('normal, standard'), derived from норма ('norm, standard, rule'), borrowed via German Norm / Polish norma from Latin norma ('carpenter's square, rule, standard'). In everyday spoken Russian, нормально commonly means 'fine, OK, doing well'.

носик.etymology: Diminutive formed with the suffix -ик from нос ('nose; prow, beak, spout'), inherited from Old East Slavic носъ and Proto-Slavic *nosъ (cognate with English nose and Latin nāsus).

history.meaning: nose → little nose; pouring spout (of a kettle or teapot)

ночь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic ночь (Old Church Slavonic нощь), from Proto-Slavic *noktь, from Proto-Indo-European *nókʷts ('night'), cognate with English night, German Nacht, French nuit, Latin nox, and Lithuanian naktìs.

ну-ка.etymology: Colloquial hortatory particle formed from the interjection/particle ну ('well, come on', inherited from Proto-Slavic *nu, cognate with English now and Latin nunc) + the enclitic particle -ка (shortened from тка / тако, used with imperatives to soften or urge an immediate action).

history.meaning: come on, let's see, go on

нужно.etymology: Neuter short-form predicate and adverbial form of нужный ('necessary, needed'), derived from нужда / нужа ('need, necessity, compulsion', from Old East Slavic нужа / Old Church Slavonic нѫжда and Proto-Slavic *nǫdja).

history.meaning: needed → (it is) necessary, one needs to

обещание.etymology: Adopted via Old Church Slavonic обѣщаниѥ ('promise, vow'), a verbal noun from обѣщати (modern обещать 'to promise'), showing the South Slavic reflex -щ- from Proto-Slavic *tj in *ob-větjati, built on *ob- + *větъ ('solemn word, declaration, counsel'; compare обет 'vow' and ответ 'answer').

обидеть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic обидѣти ('to wrong, injure, offend'), from Proto-Slavic *obiděti, reduced by haplology/dissimilation from *ob-viděti ('to look past, overlook, slight', from *ob- 'around, past' + *viděti 'to see', Russian видеть). From 'looking past someone with disregard', the meaning developed into 'to wrong, hurt, offend'.

history.meaning: to look past, slight → to wrong, offend

обидеться.etymology: Perfective reflexive verb formed by adding -ся to обидеть ('to offend, hurt'), inherited from Old East Slavic обидѣти, from Proto-Slavic *obiděti (reduced from *ob-viděti 'to look past, slight').

обижать.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of обидеть ('to offend, hurt, wrong'), continuing Old East Slavic обижати (with East Slavic ж from Proto-Slavic *dj; compare Church Slavonic обиждати), formed from *ob- ('around, past') + *viděti ('to see', Russian видеть). Originally *ob-viděti meant 'to look past someone, overlook, slight, treat with disregard', which developed into 'to wrong, offend, hurt'.

history.meaning: to overlook, slight → to wrong, offend

обижаться.etymology: Imperfective reflexive verb formed from обижать ('to offend, hurt'), continuing Old East Slavic обижати, from Proto-Slavic *obiděti / *obidjati (reduced from *ob-viděti 'to look past, slight').

обложка.etymology: Formed in Russian from обложить ('to lay around, wrap, cover') + -ка: literally the protective outer wrap laid around the pages of a book or notebook.

обман.etymology: Deverbal noun from обмануть ('to deceive, cheat'), formed from the prefix об- ('around') and the Proto-Slavic root *man- ('to beckon, lure, delude', as in манить 'to lure, entice' and Lithuanian monai 'delusion, sorcery').

обмануть.etymology: Formed with the prefix об- ('around') on the Proto-Slavic root *maniti ('to beckon, lure, delude, trick'; compare манить 'to beckon, entice' and Lithuanian monai 'witchcraft, delusion'). The consonant cluster -бм- simplified from *об-мануть, literally 'to lure around, delude with false appearances'.

обманщик.etymology: Agent noun formed in Russian with the suffix -щик from обман ('deceit, trickery') / обмануть ('to deceive, cheat', built on the Proto-Slavic root *man- 'to lure, delude').

обманывать.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of обмануть ('to deceive, cheat'), formed with the imperfectivizing suffix -ыва- on the stem обман- (from об- 'around' + Proto-Slavic *maniti 'to lure, delude, trick').
