устанавливать.etymology: Imperfective of установить ('to set up, establish, install'), formed with the prefix у- + становить ('to place, stand', causative of стать, from Proto-Slavic *stanoviti).

установленный.etymology: Past passive participle of установить ('to establish, install, set'), formed from у- + становить (from Proto-Slavic *stanoviti 'to place, set standing').

устать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic устати, from Proto-Slavic *ustati, formed from the prefix *u- ('away, completely') and *stati ('to stand, come to a standstill', Russian стать). Originally 'to come to a stop from exhaustion, to be unable to go on standing or walking'.

history.meaning: to come to a halt, grow weary

устоять.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ustojati, formed from the prefix у- ('firmly, through to the end') + стоять ('to stand', from Proto-Slavic *stojati).

устраиваться.etymology: Reflexive form of устраивать ('to arrange, organize, settle'), imperfective of устроить, derived from у- + строить ('to build, arrange, order', from строй, Proto-Slavic *strojь).

history.meaning: to get a job, settle in

устранение.etymology: Verbal noun formed with -ение from устранить ('to remove, eliminate, push aside'), a Church Slavonicism built on у- + страна ('side', corresponding to East Slavic сторона, from Proto-Slavic *storna).

устрица.etymology: Adapted with the Russian suffix -ица from earlier устерс (borrowed under Peter the Great from Dutch oesters, plural of oester), ultimately from Latin ostrea and Ancient Greek ὄστρεον (óstreon, 'oyster').

устричный.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -ный (with regular ц → ч palatalization) from устрица ('oyster').

устроить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic устроити ('to put in order, arrange, equip'), formed from у- + строить ('to build, arrange, order'), from Proto-Slavic *strojiti (from *strojь 'order, array, structure').

history.meaning: to order, build → to arrange, establish

устройство.etymology: Derived with the suffix -ство from устроить ('to arrange, construct, organize'), from у- + строить ('to build, order', from Proto-Slavic *strojiti).

уступить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic уступити ('to step back, yield'), formed from the prefix у- ('away') + ступить ('to step, tread', from Proto-Slavic *stǫpiti).

history.meaning: to yield, give in, give way

усы.etymology: Nominative plural of ус ('whisker, moustache'), inherited from Old East Slavic усъ, from Proto-Slavic *vǫsъ ('facial hair, whisker').

усыпить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic усыпити, formed from the prefix у- + causative *sypiti ('to make sleep'), from the root of спать / сон (Proto-Slavic *sъpati / *sъnъ 'sleep').

утешать.etymology: Imperfective of утешить ('to comfort, console'), inherited from Old East Slavic утѣшати / Old Church Slavonic утѣшати, from у- + тешить ('to amuse, comfort', Proto-Slavic *těšiti, causative of *tichъ 'quiet, calm').

утешить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic утѣшити ('to comfort, console'), from Proto-Slavic *utěšiti, formed from *u- + *těšiti ('to soothe, calm', etymologically related to тихий 'quiet').

утка.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic утька, diminutive of уты ('duck'), from Proto-Slavic *ǫty (genitive *ǫtъve), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂énh₂ts ('duck', cognate with Latin anas, German Ente).

утомить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic утомити, formed from the prefix у- + томить ('to weary, torment, languish', from Proto-Slavic *tomiti 'to oppress, exhaust').

утопить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic утопити, formed from the prefix у- + топить ('to sink, submerge, drown', causative of *topnǫti / тонуть, from Proto-Slavic *topiti).

утро.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic утро (alongside ютро; compare Polish jutro, where 'morning' shifted to mean 'tomorrow'), from Proto-Slavic *jutro / *utro ('dawn, morning'). Deeper connections outside Slavic remain uncertain.

утром.etymology: Lexicalized instrumental singular of утро ('morning'), used adverbially to express time when ('in the morning'). Inherited from Old East Slavic утро / ютро, from Proto-Slavic *jutro ('morning, dawn').

утюг.etymology: Borrowed from a Turkic language (compare Old Turkic ütüg, Turkish ütü 'flatiron'), derived from the Turkic verb *üt- ('to singe hair, scorch, smooth with heat').

ухажёр.etymology: Formed in Russian from ухаживать ('to court, woo, look after') + the playful French-borrowed agent suffix -ёр (modeled on дирижёр, стажёр).

history.meaning: to look after; to court, woo

ухо.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic ухо, from Proto-Slavic *uxo ('ear', plural dual *uši), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éws-os ('ear'; compare Lithuanian ausìs, Latin auris, Ancient Greek οὖς, Gothic auso, and English ear). Its irregular plural уши continues the old Slavic dual number for paired body parts.

уход.etymology: Deverbal noun formed from уходить ('to go away, leave; to tend, look after', as in уходить за кем-либо), combining the prefix у- with ход ('going, motion', from Proto-Slavic *xodъ).

history.meaning: to leave; to tend → departure, leaving; care, maintenance

уходить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic уходити ('to go away, depart'), imperfective counterpart of уйти, formed from prefix у- ('away') + ходить ('to walk, go'), from Proto-Slavic *xoditi.

ухудшать.etymology: Imperfective of ухудшить ('to worsen, make worse'), derived from у- + худший ('worse, worst', comparative/superlative of худой 'bad, meager', from Proto-Slavic *xudъ).

уцелеть.etymology: Formed with the perfective prefix у- + цел- ('whole, unharmed, intact', from целый, Proto-Slavic *cělъ) + inchoative/stative verb suffix -еть: literally 'to remain whole, come through intact'.

history.meaning: whole, intact → to survive intact, be spared

участвовать.etymology: Formed with the verbal suffix -овать from участие ('participation, share'), adopted via Old Church Slavonic оучастиѥ, built on оу- + часть ('part, share, portion', from Proto-Slavic *čęstь): literally 'to have a part or share in something'.

history.meaning: participation → to take part, participate, compete

участник.etymology: Derived with the agent suffix -ник from участие ('participation, share', from Old Church Slavonic участие, formed from у- + часть 'part, share', Proto-Slavic *čęstь).

участница.etymology: Feminine counterpart of участник ('participant'), formed with the feminine agent suffix -ница from участие ('participation', from часть 'part, share').

учебник.etymology: Formed in Russian with the object suffix -ник from учебный ('educational, teaching'), derived from учёба ('study, learning') and учить ('to teach, learn', from Proto-Slavic *učiti).

учение.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic учение / Old Church Slavonic учение ('teaching, learning, doctrine'), verbal noun of учить ('to teach, learn', from Proto-Slavic *učiti).

ученик.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic ученикъ and Old Church Slavonic оученикъ ('disciple, pupil, apprentice'), formed with the agent suffix -ик from ученъ (past passive participle of учить 'to teach', from Proto-Slavic *učiti).

history.meaning: to teach → one who is taught, pupil

учительница.etymology: Formed with the feminine agent suffix -ница from учитель ('teacher'), inherited from Old East Slavic учитель and Old Church Slavonic оучитель (from Proto-Slavic *učitelь, built on *učiti 'to teach').

учиться.etymology: Reflexive form in -ся of учить ('to teach, learn'), inherited from Old East Slavic учитися and Proto-Slavic *učiti sę ('to accustom oneself, learn'), from a causative formation on the Proto-Indo-European root *h₁ewk- ('to become accustomed', cognate with Lithuanian jaukinti 'to tame, habituate').

учредитель.etymology: Formed with the agent suffix -тель from учредить ('to found, establish, institute'), a Church Slavonicism from у- + чреда ('order, turn, sequence', corresponding to East Slavic череда, Proto-Slavic *čerda).

history.meaning: to arrange in order, institute, entertain

учёба.etymology: Derived with the nominal suffix -ёба from учить ('to teach, study', inherited from Old East Slavic учити, from Proto-Slavic *učiti).

ушастый.etymology: Derived from ухо (plural уши, stem уш-, 'ear', from Proto-Slavic *uxo) + the adjective suffix -астый ('having large or prominent...').

ущерб.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic ущербъ ('notching, waning, loss'), derived from у- + щерба ('notch, chip, gap'), from Proto-Slavic *ščьrbъ ('jagged, notched').

ущербный.etymology: Adjective formed with the suffix -ный from ущерб ('waning, loss, defect', from Proto-Slavic *ščьrbъ 'notched, chipped'), originally referring to a waning moon before developing the sense 'defective, flawed'.

уют.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ujutъ, formed from the prefix *u- + *jutъ ('shelter, lodging, roof'; compare приют 'shelter' and ютиться 'to huddle, take shelter').

уютненько.etymology: Colloquial diminutive adverb formed from уютненький, diminutive of уютный ('cozy, comfortable'), derived from уют ('coziness, shelter').

фа.etymology: Borrowed from Italian fa, the fourth solfège syllable introduced by the medieval music theorist Guido of Arezzo from the initial syllable of the Latin half-line 'Famuli tuorum' in the Hymn to St John the Baptist.

history.meaning: opening words of the fourth hymn line

фа.notes: Indeclinable neuter or feminine musical note name in Russian.

факт.etymology: Borrowed via German Fakt or French fait from Latin factum ('deed, act, something done'), substantivized neuter past participle of facere ('to do, make').

фактически.etymology: Adverb formed from фактический ('actual, factual'), derived with -еский from факт ('fact', from Latin factum).

фанат.etymology: Back-formation or clipping from фанатик ('fanatic'), reinforced in the 20th century by English fan ('sports or music enthusiast'), ultimately from Latin fanaticus ('inspired by a deity, frenzied', from fanum 'temple').

history.meaning: inspired by a temple deity, frenzied

фанатик.etymology: Borrowed via German Fanatiker or Polish fanatyk from Latin fanaticus ('belonging to a temple, inspired by a god, frenzied'), from fanum ('sanctuary, temple').

фанера.etymology: Borrowed from German Furnier ('veneer, thin wood sheet'), from French fournir ('to furnish, supply'); in late 20th-century Russian musicians' slang, петь под фанеру ('to lip-sync') arose as a phonetic play on фонограмма ('pre-recorded backing track').

фантазировать.etymology: Borrowed from German phantasieren ('to daydream, improvise, fantasize'), derived from Phantasie ('fantasy, imagination', from Ancient Greek φαντασία).

фантазия.etymology: Borrowed via Polish fantazja or German Phantasie from Latin phantasia, from Ancient Greek φαντασία (phantasía, 'appearance, image, imagination'), from φαίνω (phaínō, 'to bring to light, show').

фантазёрка.etymology: Feminine form of фантазёр ('dreamer, visionary'), formed in Russian with the suffix -ка; фантазёр combines the stem of фантазия with the French-origin agent suffix -ёр.

фантастика.etymology: Derived from фантастический / German Phantastik, ultimately from Ancient Greek φανταστικός (phantastikós, 'able to present or imagine'), from φαντασία ('imagination').

фартук.etymology: Borrowed via Polish fartuch from Middle High German vortuoch (regional German Vortuch), a compound of vor 'in front' and Tuoch 'cloth' — literally a 'fore-cloth' worn over the front of one's clothes.
фартук.notes: The second element -тук (from German Tuch 'cloth') is the same root found in галстук 'necktie' (from Halstuch 'neck-cloth').

фарш.etymology: Borrowed via German Farce or directly from French farce ('stuffing, forcemeat'), from Late Latin farsa, feminine past participle of Latin farcire ('to stuff, cram').

фейерверк.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era from German Feuerwerk ('fireworks'), a compound of Feuer ('fire') + Werk ('work').

фестиваль.etymology: Borrowed from French festival ('festival'), from Old French festival ('festive, suitable for a feast'), from Medieval Latin festivalis, from Latin festum ('feast, holiday').

фиаско.etymology: Borrowed via French fiasco from Italian fiasco ('bottle, flask'), from the Italian theatrical idiom far fiasco ('to suffer a complete failure on stage', literally 'to make a bottle').

history.meaning: to make a bottle; to fail utterly

фигня.etymology: Colloquial derivative formed with the collective/pejorative suffix -ня from фиг / фига ('fig; fig sign, nothing'), borrowed via Polish figa or German Feige from Latin ficus ('fig').

фигура.etymology: Borrowed via Polish figura from Latin figura ('form, shape, figure'), from the root of fingere ('to shape, fashion, mold').

физика.etymology: Borrowed via Latin physica (and German Physik / Polish fizyka) from Ancient Greek φυσική (ἐπιστήμη) ('knowledge of nature, natural science'), derived from φύσις ('nature', from φύω 'to grow, bring forth').

физический.etymology: Derived with the adjective suffix -еский from физика ('physics') or borrowed via German physisch from Latin physicus and Ancient Greek φυσικός (phusikós, 'natural, physical'), from φύσις (phúsis, 'nature').

фиксировать.etymology: Borrowed from German fixieren ('to fix, fasten, record'), from French fixer, derived from Latin fixus ('fixed, fast'), past participle of figere ('to fasten, fix').

фиксироваться.etymology: Reflexive and passive form of фиксировать ('to fix, record, register') formed with the enclitic -ся.

филейный.etymology: Relational adjective formed with -ный from филей / филе ('fillet, tenderloin, sirloin'), borrowed from French filet ('thin strip of meat, tenderloin'), diminutive of fil ('thread', from Latin filum).

фильм.etymology: Borrowed in the early 20th century (initially feminine фильма, later masculine фильм via German Film) from English film ('thin membrane, photographic celluloid strip, motion picture'), from Old English filmen ('membrane, skin', related to fell / pelt).

history.meaning: thin layer → celluloid roll → motion picture

финал.etymology: Borrowed via German Finale or French finale from Italian finale ('ending, conclusion'), from Latin finalis ('relating to the end'), from finis ('boundary, end').

финалистка.etymology: Feminine form of финалист ('finalist'), formed with the suffix -ка; финалист derives from финал ('final') + agent suffix -ист.

финальный.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -ный from финал ('final, finale', ultimately from Latin finalis).

финансировать.etymology: Borrowed from German finanzieren or French financer ('to finance, fund'), derived from Middle French finance ('payment, settlement, pecuniary resources', from finer 'to end, settle a debt').

финансово.etymology: Adverb formed with -о from финансовый ('financial'), derived from финансы ('finances', from French finances).

финансовый.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -овый from финансы ('finances'), borrowed via German Finanzen from French finances ('pecuniary resources, public revenue').

финиш.etymology: Borrowed in the late 19th or early 20th century from English finish ('end of a race, finishing line'), via Anglo-Norman from Old French fenir, from Latin finire ('to bound, limit, end').

финский.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -ский from финн ('Finn'), borrowed via German Finne / Swedish finne from Old Norse finnr.

фирменный.etymology: Adjective formed with -енный from фирма ('commercial firm, company, house brand'), borrowed via German Firma from Italian firma ('confirmed signature, business trade name', from Latin firmare 'to make firm, validate by signature'). In culinary and retail Russian, фирменный means 'house-special, signature, trademark'.
фирменный.notes: *Фирменное блюдо* means a restaurant's 'signature dish' or 'house speciality'.

фитнес.etymology: Borrowed in the late 20th century from English fitness ('physical fitness, exercise'), derived from fit ('healthy, well-suited') + -ness.

фишка.etymology: Adapted with the Russian suffix -ка from French fiche ('gaming counter, peg, token', originally a pointed peg used in games), from ficher ('to fix, drive in', from Vulgar Latin *figicare).

фламбе.etymology: Borrowed from French flambé ('flamed, singed'), past participle of flamber ('to flame, blaze'), from flambe / flamme ('flame', from Latin flamma).

флеш.etymology: Borrowed from English flush (in card games, a hand of cards all of the same suit), related to flush ('full, even, abundant').

history.meaning: hand of cards of one suit

флешка.etymology: Colloquial Russian formation with the suffix -ка from флеш-память / флеш-накопитель, borrowed from English flash drive / flash memory (named because memory blocks are erased in a 'flash').

фмс.etymology: Initialism of Федеральная миграционная служба ('Federal Migration Service'), the Russian government agency overseeing migration from 1992 to 2016.

фокусник.etymology: Formed with the agent suffix -ник from фокус ('magic trick, sleight of hand'), shortened from German Hokuspokus ('hocus-pocus, conjurer's formula').

фонарик.etymology: Formed in Russian as the diminutive of фонарь ('street lamp, lantern') with suffix -ик; фонарь itself comes from Byzantine Greek φανάριον ('lantern'). Today фонарик means both a small decorative lantern and a handheld pocket flashlight.

фонарь.etymology: Borrowed into Old East Slavic (фонарь) from Byzantine Greek φανάριον (phanárion), diminutive of Ancient Greek φανός ('torch, lantern'), from φαίνω ('to shine, bring to light', related to English phantom and phenomenon).

фондан.etymology: Borrowed from French fondant ('melting', short for chocolat fondant or gâteau au chocolat fondant), present participle of fondre ('to melt', from Latin fundere 'to pour, melt').

фонтан.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via Italian fontana (or Polish fontanna) from Late Latin fontāna ('spring, fountain'), substantivized feminine of fontānus ('of a spring'), from Latin fōns, fontis ('spring, source of water').

фора.etymology: Borrowed via German Vorgabe or directly from Italian fora / fuori ('outside, ahead', in billiards and games), or German vor ('ahead, in front'), denoting points or time given in advance as a handicap.

форма.etymology: Borrowed via Polish forma (and German Form) from Latin fōrma ('shape, figure, mould, stamp, last'). In Russian it means outer 'shape, form', a school or military 'uniform', and a culinary 'baking tin, cake mould'.

history.meaning: shape, form; baking tin, mould; uniform

формально.etymology: Adverb formed from формальный ('formal'), borrowed via Polish formalny from Latin formalis ('relating to form, formal'), from forma ('shape, form, rule').

формат.etymology: Borrowed via German Format or French format from Italian formato ('size and shape of a book'), from Latin (liber) formatus ('shaped book', from formare 'to form, shape').

формула.etymology: Borrowed from Latin formula ('small form, mold, rule, fixed form of words'), diminutive of forma ('form, shape').

форточка.etymology: Borrowed from German Pfortchen ('little door', diminutive of Pforte 'gate, door'), or via Polish fortka from the same German word, ultimately from Latin porta 'gate, door'. In Russian homes it came to name the small hinged pane set into a larger window frame for airing a room in winter.
форточка.notes: Открыть форточку is the classic way to let fresh air into a warm room without opening the whole casement.

форум.etymology: Borrowed from Latin forum ('public square, marketplace, assembly place in ancient Rome'), akin to foris ('outside, out of doors').

фото.etymology: Clipped indeclinable noun from фотография ('photography, photograph'), formed from the international Greek-derived compound photo- (from Ancient Greek φῶς, φωτός 'light') + -graphia ('drawing, writing').
фото.notes: Indeclinable neuter noun in Russian: старое фото ('an old photo').

фотограф.etymology: Borrowed from German Photograph or French photographe, coined from Ancient Greek φῶς, φωτός (phôs, phōtós, 'light') + -γράφος (-gráphos, 'writer, drawer', from γράφω 'to write, draw').

фотографировать.etymology: Borrowed from German photographieren or formed in Russian from фотография ('photography') + the verbal suffix -ировать.

фоторобот.etymology: Borrowed from French portrait-robot (adapted in Russian with фото- 'photo-' + робот 'robot', coined by French police commissioner Pierre Chabot in the 1950s for a composite facial sketch assembled from photographic strips).

фотошоп.etymology: Borrowed from English Photoshop, the trademarked name of the raster graphics editor Adobe Photoshop (created in 1988 by Thomas and John Knoll from photo + shop).

фраза.etymology: Borrowed via French phrase or German Phrase from Late Latin phrasis, from Ancient Greek φράσις ('way of speaking, expression, phrase'), derived from φράζω ('to point out, declare, express').

фрак.etymology: Borrowed via French frac and German Frack from English frock ('men's coat, smock, tunic', from Old French froc).

француз.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th–17th centuries via Polish Francuz (influenced by French François / Français and German Franzose), ultimately from Late Latin Francus ('Frank').

фреш.etymology: Borrowed in the late 20th century from English fresh (short for freshly squeezed juice), from Old French freis and Proto-Germanic *friskaz.

фрикасе.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th–19th century from French fricassée ('dish of white meat cut into pieces and stewed in a white sauce'), the feminine past participle of fricasser ('to cut up and cook in sauce'), traditionally explained in French etymology as a blend of frire ('to fry', from Latin frīgere) and casser ('to break into pieces', from Late Latin quassāre).

history.meaning: meat cut into pieces and braised in white sauce

фуа-гра.etymology: Borrowed from French foie gras (literally 'fat liver'), from foie ('liver', from Late Latin ficatum 'fig-fattened liver') + gras ('fat', from Latin crassus).

фугу.etymology: Borrowed via English fugu from Japanese 河豚 (fugu, 'pufferfish, blowfish').

фуд-стилист.etymology: Borrowed in the 21st century from English food stylist (a compound of food + stylist, a specialist who arranges dishes for photography or film).

функция.etymology: Borrowed via Polish funkcja or German Funktion from Latin functio ('performance, execution, duty'), derived from fungi ('to perform, execute, discharge').

фура.etymology: Borrowed via Polish fura ('wagon, cartload') from Middle High German vuore / German Fuhre ('wagon, cartload, haul'), from the root of fahren ('to drive, travel').

фургон.etymology: Borrowed from French fourgon ('covered baggage wagon, delivery van'), a word of uncertain Romance/Germanic origin originally denoting a long-poled baggage cart following an army.

фуршет.etymology: Shortened from French (déjeuner) à la fourchette ('(meal eaten) with a fork', i.e. a standing reception where guests eat with forks without sitting at a table), from fourchette ('fork', diminutive of fourche, from Latin furca).

футбол.etymology: Borrowed in the late 19th century from English football, a compound of foot and ball.

футболка.etymology: Formed in Russian with the suffix -ка from футбол ('football, soccer', from English football), originally denoting a jersey worn by football players before generalizing to any T-shirt.

ха.etymology: Primary vocalic interjection imitating the open-mouthed exhalation of laughter or sudden exclamation, with parallels across Slavic and Indo-European languages (compare English ha!).

халат.etymology: Borrowed via Turkic (compare Turkish hilat, Tatar xalat) from Arabic خِلْعَة (ḵilʿa, 'robe of honor bestowed by a ruler'), from خَلَعَ (ḵalaʿa, 'to take off clothes to bestow as a gift').

хам.etymology: From the biblical name Хам ('Ham', son of Noah in Genesis 9:22, who mocked his father's nakedness), borrowed via Old Church Slavonic Хамъ and Greek Χάμ from Hebrew חָם (Ḥām), used in Russian first for serfs and later for any insolent boor.

хан.etymology: Borrowed into Old East Slavic (ханъ / канъ) from Turkic and Mongolic khan / qan ('ruler, sovereign, prince').

хана.etymology: Colloquial slang word borrowed via criminal argot (Odessa/fenya), most likely from Yiddish חנה (khane) or Hebrew חֲנָה (ḥănā, 'encampment, stopping place, end of the road'), or Turkic xana ('house, shelter, final station').

характер.etymology: Borrowed via Polish charakter and German Charakter from Latin character, from Ancient Greek χαρακτήρ (kharaktḗr, 'engraved mark, stamp, distinctive nature'), from χαράσσω (kharássō, 'to sharpen, engrave').

хачапури.etymology: Borrowed from Georgian ხაჭაპური (xač̣ap̣uri, 'cheese bread'), a compound of ხაჭო (xač̣o, 'curd, cottage cheese') + პური (p̣uri, 'bread').

хачапурщик.etymology: Formed in Russian with the occupational agent suffix -щик from хачапури ('khachapuri, Georgian cheese bread').

хватить.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *xvatiti ('to snatch, seize, reach'). From the concrete sense 'to grasp, reach far enough' developed the common impersonal sense хватит ('it suffices, that is enough!').

хватка.etymology: Derived with the nominal suffix -ка from хватать ('to grasp, seize, snatch', inherited from Proto-Slavic *xvatati).

хитрец.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic хитрьць (originally 'craftsman, skilled artisan, wise man'), formed with the agent suffix -ец from хитрый ('clever, skillful, cunning', from Proto-Slavic *xytrъ).

хитроумный.etymology: Compound adjective formed from хитрый ('cunning, clever, skillful') + connecting vowel -о- + ум ('mind, wit') + -ный, modeled as a calque of Ancient Greek πολύμητις / ἀγκυλομήτης ('of crooked/clever counsel').

хитрый.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic хитрыи (and Old Church Slavonic хꙑтръ 'skillful, clever, ingenious, artful'), from Proto-Slavic *xytrъ, originally a *-ro- adjective derived from the same root as хватать / похитить ('to seize, snatch, grasp quickly', Proto-Slavic *xytiti). From 'quick to grasp, dexterous, skillful' (still preserved in нехитрый 'simple, uncomplicated'), the meaning shifted to 'crafty, cunning, sly'.

хлам.etymology: Connected by Vasmer with Proto-Slavic *xlamъ / *xolomъ ('heap, mound, debris'; compare dialectal холомить 'to heap up carelessly' and холм 'hill').

хлеб.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic хлѣбъ, from Proto-Slavic *xlěbъ, widely regarded by Vasmer and modern Slavicists as an early borrowing from Proto-Germanic *hlaibaz ('baked loaf', the ancestor of Gothic hlaifs and English loaf).

хлопать.etymology: Expressive Slavic onomatopoeic verb built on the sound-symbolic root *xlop- imitating a flat slap, clap of hands, or banging of a door (compare Polish chłapać and Ukrainian хлопати).

хлопковый.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -овый from хло́пок ('cotton'), which developed in Russian from dialectal охло́пок ('tuft, flock of tow or fibres'), reshaped under the influence of хлопать.

хлопок.etymology: Derived with the suffix -ок from хлопать ('to clap, bang, pop'), denoting a single sharp clap, pop, or bang (stressed хлопо́к). (A homograph stressed хло́пок means 'cotton', reshaped from dialectal охлопок 'tuft of tow or fibres'.)

history.meaning: to clap, bang → a clap, pop, bang

хлопок.notes: Watch the stress difference: **хлопо́к** (genitive хлопка́) means 'a clap, pop, bang', whereas **хло́пок** (genitive хло́пка) means 'cotton'.

хлопоты.etymology: Plural-only noun (singular хлопота in older and dialectal Russian), derived from the expressive Slavic stem *xlopotъ ('bustling noise, clatter, busyness'), related to хлопать ('to bang, bustle about').

хм.etymology: Onomatopoeic vocal gesture imitating a closed-lip throat clearing or nasal hum expressing thoughtfulness, hesitation, or mild doubt (parallel to English hm / hmph).

history.meaning: hm, hmph (interjection of thought or doubt)

хобби.etymology: Borrowed in the mid-20th century from English hobby ('leisure pastime'), shortened from hobbyhorse ('toy horse, favorite pastime'), itself from Hob / Robin (pet forms of Robert).

ход.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic ходъ ('walking, motion, procession, way'), from Proto-Slavic *xodъ, a deverbal noun associated with *xoditi ('to walk, go', Russian ходить; Vasmer compares Ancient Greek ὁδός hodós 'way, road, journey' from PIE *sod-o-).

history.meaning: motion, course; move/turn (in a game); entrance

хозяйство.etymology: Derived with the suffix -ство from хозяин ('master, host, owner'), a borrowing into Russian from a Turkic language (compare Kipchak/Tatar xojayin, ultimately from Persian خواجه xwāja 'master, lord').

холл.etymology: Borrowed in the late nineteenth or twentieth century from English hall ('entrance hall, hotel lobby, lounge').

холм.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic хълмъ ('hill, mound'), from Proto-Slavic *xъlmъ, an early borrowing from Proto-Germanic *hulmaz ('rising ground, hill, small island', cognate with Old English holm and ultimately related to Latin collis 'hill').

холодец.etymology: Formed with the noun suffix -ец from холодный ('cold') / холод ('cold', from Proto-Slavic *xoldъ), denoting meat broth chilled until it sets into a savory jelly.

хомячить.etymology: Colloquial denominal verb formed with -ить from хомяк ('hamster', from Old East Slavic хомякъ, Proto-Slavic *xoměkъ), alluding to how a hamster stuffs its cheek pouches with food.

хоромы.etymology: Plural of archaic хорома, inherited from Old East Slavic хоромы ('wooden house, mansion'), from Proto-Slavic *xormъ ('house, building, shelter'; compare Old Church Slavonic храмъ, source of Russian храм 'temple').

хоронить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic хоронити ('to guard, keep safe, hide away, bury'), from Proto-Slavic *xorniti ('to protect, shelter, put away'), showing regular East Slavic pleophony -оро- alongside the Church Slavonic doublet хранить ('to keep, preserve').

хороший.etymology: Attested in Old Russian from the 13th century (хорошии), replacing older добрый in many everyday contexts for 'good'. Its deeper origin is uncertain: Vasmer reviews competing proposals, including a shortened expressive form of хоробрый ('brave, fine') or derivation from proper names.

хостес.etymology: Borrowed in the late 20th century from English hostess ('female host welcoming guests at a restaurant or event'), from Old French hostesse.

history.meaning: female host at a restaurant or flight

хотя.etymology: Originally the present adverbial participle (gerund) of хотеть ('to want, wish', from Old East Slavic хотѣти and Proto-Slavic *xotěti): literally 'even wishing / granting that...', which grammaticalized into the concessive conjunction 'although, even though' (and with бы: хотя бы 'at least, even if').

history.meaning: although, even though (хотя бы: at least)

хохма.etymology: Borrowed via Yiddish חכמה (khokhme, 'wisdom; witty remark, joke, prank') from Hebrew חָכְמָה (ḥoḵmā, 'wisdom, cleverness').

храм.etymology: Borrowed in its Old Church Slavonic non-pleophonic form храмъ ('house, temple, church'), corresponding to native East Slavic хоромы ('large wooden mansion, house', with pleophony -оро-), from Proto-Slavic *xormъ ('building, house, shelter'). While East Slavic хоромы kept the secular meaning 'spacious residence', the elevated Church Slavonic form храм specialized to mean 'temple, cathedral, house of worship'.

хранитель.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic хранитель ('guardian, keeper'), formed with the agent suffix -тель from хранити ('to guard, keep', from Proto-Slavic *xorniti).

храниться.etymology: Reflexive and passive form of хранить ('to keep, store, preserve', a Church Slavonicism corresponding to East Slavic хоронить, from Proto-Slavic *xorniti) + -ся.

хрупкий.etymology: Derived with the adjectival suffix -кий from the Slavic expressive stem *xrup- ('to crack, crunch, snap easily'; compare Old East Slavic хрупати 'to crunch, crack' and Polish chrupki 'crisp, brittle').

хрустеть.etymology: Inherited from East Slavic хрустѣти, built on the Proto-Slavic onomatopoeic root *xrust- ('crunch, crackle, rustle'; compare Old Church Slavonic хроустание 'gnashing, crunching' and Polish chrzęścić).

хрустящий.etymology: Present active participle in -ящий of хрустеть ('to crunch, crackle, rustle'), lexicalized as the standard culinary adjective 'crisp, crunchy, crusty'.

хряк.etymology: Of onomatopoeic Slavic origin (compare Ukrainian кряк / хряк, Polish chrząkać 'to grunt'), imitating the deep grunting sound of a male hog (related to хрюкать 'to oink, grunt').

худой.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic худыи ('poor, bad, meager, thin'), from Proto-Slavic *xudъ ('small, poor, thin, bad').

худший.etymology: Comparative and superlative adjective inherited from Old East Slavic хужьшии (influenced by Church Slavonic хуждшии), formed from худой ('bad, poor', Proto-Slavic *xudъ) + comparative suffix *-jьš-.

хуже.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic хуже, comparative degree of худой ('bad, poor; thin'), from Proto-Slavic *xudъ ('poor, small, bad, meager') + the comparative suffix *-jьše (with regular palatalization *dj → ж).
хуже.notes: In modern Russian, *хуже* serves as the standard comparative of *плохой* ('bad') and *плохо* ('badly').

хэллоуин.etymology: Borrowed from English Halloween, contracted from Scottish All-Hallows-Even ('All Hallows' Eve', the evening before All Saints' Day, from hallow 'saint, holy person' + even 'evening').

хэппи-энд.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English happy end / happy ending ('favorable resolution of a story or film').

царапина.etymology: Formed with the singulative result suffix -ина from царапать ('to scratch, claw, scrape'), an expressive East Slavic onomatopoeic verb imitating the rasping sound of claws or a sharp point on a surface.

history.meaning: to scratch → a scratch, scrape mark

цвет.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic цвѣтъ ('blossom, flower; bright hue, colour'), from Proto-Slavic *květъ ('flower, bloom'), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱweyt- ('to shine, be bright'). In Russian the plural splits the two senses: цвета́ ('colours') vs. цветы́ ('flowers').

цветочный.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -ный from цветок ('flower', stem цветк- with regular k → ч alternation before -н-), itself the diminutive of цвет ('blossom, flower', from Proto-Slavic *květъ).

цедра.etymology: Borrowed in the eighteenth century from Italian cedro ('citron, cedar-citron fruit', from Latin citrus and Ancient Greek κέδρος). In Russian culinary usage, цедра narrowed specifically to the fragrant outer coloured peel ('zest') of a lemon, orange, or lime.

целиком.etymology: Frozen instrumental singular of целик ('whole, untouched piece or virgin soil'), derived with the suffix -ик from целый ('whole, intact', from Proto-Slavic *cělъ).

целовать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic цѣловати ('to greet, wish good health; to kiss in greeting'), from Proto-Slavic *cělovati, a denominative verb formed from *cělъ ('whole, intact, healthy, hale', modern Russian целый, cognate with English whole and hale). Originally целовать meant 'to wish someone wholeness/health (цел будь!)' upon meeting, accompanied by the customary ritual kiss of greeting; the verb then transferred to the physical act of kissing itself.

history.meaning: whole, hale → to greet with a wish of health

цена.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic цѣна ('price, value, worth'), from Proto-Slavic *cěna ('compensation, price, value'), from Proto-Indo-European *kʷoynéh₂ ('recompense, penalty, price', cognate with Ancient Greek ποινή 'blood-price, penalty' and Lithuanian kaina 'price').

ценить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic цѣнити ('to set a price on, value, appraise'), a denominative verb formed from цѣна / цена ('price, value, worth', historically also 'bloodwite, compensation'), from Proto-Slavic *cěna ('price, compensation, value', from PIE *kʷoyneh₂ 'recompense, price', cognate with Lithuanian kainà 'price' and Ancient Greek ποινή poinḗ 'compensation, penalty').

ценник.etymology: Formed in Russian with the suffix -ник from ценный / цена ('price, value', inherited from Old East Slavic цѣна, from Proto-Slavic *cěna).

ценный.etymology: Adjective formed with the suffix -ный from цена ('price, value, worth', inherited from Old East Slavic цѣна, from Proto-Slavic *cěna).

центр.etymology: Borrowed via German Zentrum / French centre from Latin centrum ('centre of a circle, stationary pivot point of a pair of compasses'), from Ancient Greek κέντρον ('sharp point, goad, stationary point of a compass', from κεντέω 'to prick').

history.meaning: sharp point, pivot of a compass

центральный.etymology: Borrowed via Polish centralny or German zentral from Latin centralis ('in the middle, central'), from centrum ('center', from Ancient Greek κέντρον kéntron 'sharp point, stationary point of a compass').

центрифуга.etymology: Borrowed from German Zentrifuge, back-formed from New Latin centrifugus ('fleeing from the center'), coined by Isaac Newton from centrum ('center') + fugere ('to flee').

цеплять.etymology: Iterative/imperfective of цепить ('to hook, catch, fasten'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *cěpiti / *čepiti ('to hook, seize, split'; related to цепь 'chain').

history.meaning: to hook, snag; to pick on, needle

цепочка.etymology: Diminutive formed with the suffix -очка from цепь ('chain'), inherited from Old East Slavic чепь / цѣпь ('chain', from Proto-Slavic *čepь).

церемония.etymology: Borrowed via Polish ceremonia or German Zeremonie from Latin caerimonia ('sacredness, religious rite, ritual observance').

церковь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic цьркы (accusative цьрковь, which became the modern nominative церковь), from Proto-Slavic *cьrky (genitive *cьrkъve), an early Germanic borrowing (from Old Bavarian *kirko / Old High German kirihha, cognate with English church and German Kirche), which itself came from Late Greek κυριακόν (kyriakón, '[house] of the Lord', from κύριος kýrios 'lord').

цирк.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th–19th century via German Zirkus / French cirque from Latin circus ('circle, ring, oval arena for chariot races and public spectacles, such as the Circus Maximus'), related to Ancient Greek κρίκος / κίρκος (kírkos, 'ring, circle').

history.meaning: circle, circular arena for public games

цитадель.etymology: Borrowed via French citadelle or German Zitadelle from Italian cittadella ('fortress commanding a city', literally 'little city'), diminutive of cittade / città ('city', from Latin civitas).

цифра.etymology: Borrowed via Polish cyfra and German Ziffer from Medieval Latin cifra ('zero; numerical figure'), ultimately from Arabic ṣifr ('empty, zero', from ṣafira 'to be empty') — the same Arabic source that gave English cipher and zero.

цукини.etymology: Borrowed via English or German from Italian zucchine / zucchini ('small squashes'), plural of zucchino, diminutive of zucca ('gourd, pumpkin, squash').

чаепитие.etymology: Compound noun formed in Russian from чай ('tea') + linking vowel -е- + питие ('drinking', bookish/Slavonic verbal noun from пить 'to drink'): literally 'tea-drinking, a sociable tea gathering'.

чай.etymology: Borrowed in the 17th century via overland caravan trade across Mongolia and Turkic intermediaries from Northern Mandarin 茶 (chá). Languages supplied overland kept the cha- form (Russian чай, Arabic shāy), whereas maritime trade from Fujian carried Min Nan tê into Western European tea and thé.

чайный.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -ный from чай ('tea'), borrowed in the seventeenth century via Central Asian/Mongolic trade routes from Northern Chinese 茶 (chá).

чапать.etymology: Colloquial East Slavic verb of onomatopoeic origin (*čapati), imitating the heavy, splashing, or shuffling sound of footsteps (also related to dialectal чапать 'to grab, step').

час.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic часъ ('time, moment, hour'), from Proto-Slavic *časъ, compared by Vasmer with Old Prussian kīsman ('time') and the Slavic root of чаяти ('to wait, watch for'). Its plural часы came to mean a timepiece — a clock or wristwatch.

часик.etymology: Diminutive formed with the suffix -ик from час ('hour, time', inherited from Old East Slavic часъ, from Proto-Slavic *časъ).

часовой.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -овой from час ('hour') and its plural часы ('clock, watch'), inherited from Old East Slavic часъ ('time, hour', from Proto-Slavic *časъ).

history.meaning: hour / clock → hour-long; clock, watch (часовой механизм 'clockwork')

часовщик.etymology: Formed in Russian from часы 'clock, watch' (plural of час 'hour') + the craftsperson suffix -овщик: one who makes and mends clocks and watches.

часок.etymology: Diminutive formed with the suffix -ок from час ('hour, time', inherited from Old East Slavic часъ, from Proto-Slavic *časъ).

частично.etymology: Adverb formed from частичный ('partial'), derived from частица / часть ('part, portion, share', inherited from Old East Slavic часть, from Proto-Slavic *čęstь).

частный.etymology: Derived with the adjectival suffix -ный from часть ('part, individual share'), inherited from Old East Slavic часть ('part, portion') and Proto-Slavic *čęstь: literally 'pertaining to a particular part or individual, private' (as opposed to общий 'common, general').
частный.notes: The middle -т- is silent in standard pronunciation: pronounced [ча́сный].

часто.etymology: Adverb formed from the neuter short form of частый ('frequent; thick, dense, closely spaced'), inherited from Old East Slavic частыи (and Old Church Slavonic чѧстъ 'dense, frequent'), from Proto-Slavic *čęstъ ('packed together, dense', as in чаща 'dense forest thicket', cognate with Lithuanian kim̃štas 'stuffed, crammed'). What is packed closely together in space ('dense trees') is 'frequent, often' in time.

часть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic часть ('part, share, portion, lot'), from Proto-Slavic *čęstь ('piece cut or bitten off, share'), related to кусок ('piece') and кусать ('to bite') via nasal ablaut (*kǫs- / *čęst-).

чаша.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic чаша and Old Church Slavonic чаша ('bowl, goblet, basin'), from Proto-Slavic *čaša, cognate with Old Prussian kiosi ('goblet') and compared by Vasmer to Iranian/Indo-Iranian words for a drinking bowl (compare Persian kāse 'bowl').

history.meaning: basin (of a fountain or scales), large bowl, chalice

чашечка.etymology: Double diminutive formed with -ечка from чашка ('cup'), itself a diminutive of чаша ('bowl, chalice, cup', inherited from Old East Slavic чаша, from Proto-Slavic *čaša).

чаще.etymology: Comparative degree of частый ('frequent, thick') and часто ('often'), inherited from Old East Slavic чаще (Proto-Slavic *čęstjьše, with regular palatalization of *stj → щ), from Proto-Slavic *čęstъ ('dense, close-packed, frequent').

чаёк.etymology: Affectionate/partitive diminutive formed with the suffix -ёк from чай ('tea', borrowed in the 17th century via Mongolic/Turkic čaj from Mandarin Chinese 茶 chá).

history.meaning: some tea, a nice cup of tea

чебурек.etymology: Borrowed from Crimean Tatar çüberek ('deep-fried meat turnover'), formed from çiy ('raw', referring to the raw minced meat filling before frying) + börek ('filled pastry, turnover').

чебуречная.etymology: Substantivized feminine relational adjective formed with -ная from чебурек ('cheburek'), on the pattern of булочная, пельменная, and чайная.

чей-то.etymology: Indefinite possessive pronoun formed from чей ('whose', inherited from Old East Slavic чии, from Proto-Slavic *čьjь) + the indefinite enclitic particle -то (from the demonstrative pronoun то, Proto-Slavic *to).

человеческий.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic человѣчьскыи / Old Church Slavonic чловѣчьскъ, formed with the adjective suffix -еский from человек ('person, human', from Proto-Slavic *čelověkъ).

чемодан.etymology: Borrowed into Russian via Turkic languages (compare Tatar çumadan) from Persian jāmedān ('wardrobe, travelling clothes-bag'), a compound of jāme ('garment, cloth') and the container suffix -dān ('holder'). Originally a soft saddlebag or cloth bundle case, it came to mean a rigid travelling suitcase.

чемодан-близнец.etymology: Hyphenated appositional compound of чемодан ('suitcase', borrowed via Turkic from Persian jāmedān 'garment-holder') + близнец ('twin', from Old East Slavic близньць, derived from близъ 'near, close').

чемоданчик.etymology: Diminutive formed with the suffix -чик from чемодан ('suitcase, trunk'), borrowed via Turkic (compare Tatar čamadan, Turkish camadan) from Persian جامه‌دان (jāma-dān, 'wardrobe, clothes-holder', from jāma 'garment' + -dān 'container').

чемпион.etymology: Borrowed from English champion or French champion ('combatant, winner of a contest'), from Medieval Latin campio ('gladiator, fighter in the field'), derived from Latin campus ('field, arena').

чемпионат.etymology: Borrowed from French championnat ('championship tournament'), derived from champion ('champion') + the suffix -at.

чемпионка.etymology: Feminine counterpart of чемпион ('champion'), formed in Russian with the feminine suffix -ка.

чердак.etymology: Borrowed via Turkic čardak ('upper gallery, balcony, garret under the roof') from Persian čārdāq / čahār-tāq ('four-pillared pavilion or upper roof structure', from čahār 'four' + tāq 'arch, vault').

черевички.etymology: Plural of черевичек, diminutive of черевик ('high-heeled leather boot or shoe', borrowed from or shared with Ukrainian черевики), inherited from Old East Slavic черевикъ ('leather shoe'), derived from черево ('belly, soft belly leather', from Proto-Slavic *červo).

череп.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic черепъ (originally 'potsherd, earthenware shell', later 'skull'), from Proto-Slavic *čerpъ ('sherd, shell, skull'), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kerp- ('to cut, scrape').

черепаха.etymology: Derived in East Slavic with the suffix -аха from череп ('shell, sherd, hard carapace', from Proto-Slavic *čerpъ), literally 'the shelled creature' (replacing older желы / желвь).

черепаховый.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -овый from черепаха ('turtle, tortoise').

чернила.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic чьрнило, formed from чернить ('to blacken, make dark', from чёрный 'black') + the substance/instrument suffix -ило; settled in modern Russian as a plural-only noun.
чернила.notes: Even though чернила literally comes from 'blackening fluid', Russian freely speaks of синие чернила ('blue ink') and красные чернила ('red ink').

черничный.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -ный (with к → ч palatalization) from черника ('blueberry, bilberry'), itself derived from чёрный ('black, dark', Proto-Slavic *čьrnъ) after the dark stain of its juice.

чертовщина.etymology: Derived with the collective/abstract suffix -щина from чёртов ('devil's, diabolical'), possessive adjective of чёрт ('devil, demon', from Proto-Slavic *čьrtъ).

чертёж.etymology: Formed in Russian (attested since the sixteenth century for early Muscovite maps and plans) with the noun suffix -ёж from чертить ('to draw lines, draft'), built on черта ('drawn line, incised mark', from Proto-Slavic *čьrta, from the root of черкать 'to scratch, incise').

history.meaning: to draw lines → map, architectural plan

чесать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic чесати ('to comb, card wool, scratch, strip'), from Proto-Slavic *česati ('to comb, scratch, scrape'); the colloquial sense 'to stride briskly, hurry off' developed metaphorically from vigorous repetitive strokes.

history.meaning: to scratch, comb; (slang) to hurry off

чесаться.etymology: Reflexive form in -ся of чесать ('to scratch, comb'), inherited from Old East Slavic чесати and Proto-Slavic *česati ('to scratch, comb, card wool'). In the reflexive it means both 'to scratch oneself' and 'to itch'.

history.meaning: to scratch → to itch; to scratch oneself

чеснок.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic чеснокъ / чеснъкъ, derived with the suffix -ок from Proto-Slavic *česnъ ('garlic, split bulb'), from *česati ('to split, tear off, comb'), referring to a bulb that splits into cloves.

четверг.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic четвьрьгъ ('Thursday'), formed from четвьртыи ('fourth', from четыре 'four', Proto-Slavic *četyre): literally 'the fourth day' of the week counting from Monday.

history.meaning: fourth day of the week, Thursday

четверо.etymology: Collective numeral inherited from Old East Slavic четверо, from Proto-Slavic *četvero ('group of four'), from Proto-Indo-European *kʷetwóres ('four').

четверть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic четвьрть ('quarter, fourth part'), from Proto-Slavic *četvьrtь, an abstract fraction noun built on *četvьrtъ ('fourth', from *četyre 'four').

четыреста.etymology: Compound numeral inherited from Old East Slavic четыре съта ('four hundreds'), combining четыре ('four', from Proto-Slavic *četyre) + ста (nominative/accusative dual-plural form of сто 'hundred', from Proto-Slavic *sъto).

четырнадцатый.etymology: Ordinal numeral formed from четырнадцать ('fourteen'), contracted from Old East Slavic четырь на десяте ('four upon ten', from Proto-Slavic *četyre na desęte).

четырнадцать.etymology: Contracted in East Slavic from the Old East Slavic phrase четыри на десяте ('four upon ten'), from Proto-Slavic *četyre na desęte.

четырёхконечный.etymology: Compound adjective formed from четырёх (genitive of четыре 'four', from Proto-Slavic *četyre) + конечный ('-pointed, -ended', from конец 'end, point', Proto-Slavic *konьcь).

чечевица.etymology: Developed by consonant assimilation (с...ч -> ч...ч) from Old East Slavic сочевица, built on сочиво 'lentil seed, pulse dish', from Proto-Slavic *sočivo and related to сок 'juice, sap'.
чечевица.notes: Singular only as a collective food noun in Russian: варить чечевицу 'to cook lentils'.

чинить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic чинити ('to arrange, put in order, make, repair'), from Proto-Slavic *činiti, a denominative verb from *činъ ('order, rank, proper arrangement'). From 'putting back into proper order' came the modern everyday sense 'to repair, mend, sharpen (a pencil)'.

history.meaning: order, arrangement → to put in order, make

чипсы.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English chips (plural of chip, in potato chips 'thin fried slices of potato').

чистить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic чистити ('to clean, purify'), from Proto-Slavic *čistiti, a factitive verb built on *čistъ ('clean, pure', modern чистый).

history.meaning: to clean, polish, brush; to peel (fruit, vegetables)

чистка.etymology: Verbal action noun formed with the suffix -ка from чистить ('to clean, brush, polish'), derived from чистый ('clean', from Proto-Slavic *čistъ).

чисто.etymology: Adverbial and predicate form in -о of чистый ('clean, pure'), from Old East Slavic чисто and Proto-Slavic *čisto.

чистоплотный.etymology: Compound adjective formed from чистый ('clean, pure', Proto-Slavic *čistъ) + -о- + плоть ('flesh, body', Proto-Slavic *plъtь) + -ный, literally 'clean-bodied'.

что-нибудь.etymology: Indefinite pronoun formed in Russian by joining что ('what', from Proto-Slavic *čьto) with the indefinite particle -нибудь (contracted from ни будь 'whatever it may be', built on ни + будь, imperative of быть 'to be').

чтобы.etymology: Fused in East Slavic from the pronoun/conjunction что ('what, that', from Proto-Slavic *čьto) + the conditional/subjunctive particle бы (originally an aorist form of быть 'to be').

чувак.etymology: 20th-century Russian youth slang (popularized by the 1950s stilyagi subculture); most widely traced by linguists to Romani čhavo ('boy, lad, Romani youth'; compare British slang chav), though folk etymologies and competing hypotheses connect it with dialectal or Turkic words.

чувствовать.etymology: Derived with the verbal suffix -овать from чувство ('feeling, sense'), borrowed or reshaped via Old Church Slavonic чоувьство from Proto-Slavic *čuvьstvo, built on *čuti ('to perceive, hear, sense, feel'; compare чуть and чуять).
чувствовать.notes: The first -в- in *чувствовать* and *чувство* is silent in standard pronunciation ([чу́ствавать]).

чудесный.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic чудесьныи and Old Church Slavonic чоудесьнъ ('miraculous, wonderful'), formed with the adjectival suffix -ный on the ancient consonant stem чудес- of чудо ('miracle, wonder', plural чудеса, from Proto-Slavic *čudo, genitive *čudese).

чудный.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic чудьныи ('marvelous, wondrous; strange'), derived with the suffix -ный from чудо ('miracle, wonder, marvel', from Proto-Slavic *čudo).

чудо.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic чудо and Proto-Slavic *čudo 'wonder, marvel', cognate with Ancient Greek kudos 'glory, renown' — originally something remarkable that people hear of and marvel at.
чудо.notes: Preserves the ancient Slavic -ес- stem in the plural: чудо -> чудеса, чудес.

чудо-капли.etymology: Compound noun formed in Russian from чудо ('miracle, wonder', from Proto-Slavic *čudo) + капли ('drops', plural of капля, from Proto-Slavic *kapľa).

чур.etymology: Exclamation of boundary or protective warding ('hands off!, dibs!, touch wood!'), inherited from Old East Slavic чуръ ('border, boundary mark, protective limit'; compare пращур 'forefather' and чураться 'to shun').

чуть.etymology: Originally the shortened infinitive (or supine) чути / чуть ('to perceive, hear, sense faintly'), from Proto-Slavic *čuti ('to sense, feel'). From phrases like чуть слышно ('barely audible to the senses') it grammaticalized into the adverb 'barely, slightly, a little'.

history.meaning: to perceive faintly → barely, slightly, a little

чушь.etymology: Likely altered from чужь ('something alien, strange, outlandish', abstract feminine noun from чужой 'foreign, strange', Proto-Slavic *ťudjь), or connected with dialectal чухать / чушка.

чёртов.etymology: Possessive adjective formed with the suffix -ов from чёрт ('devil, demon'), inherited from Old East Slavic чьртъ, from Proto-Slavic *čьrtъ.

чёткий.etymology: Derived with the adjectival suffix -кий from чёт ('even number, exact tally') and читать / честь ('to count, read', from Proto-Slavic *čьt-). Originally 'easy to read or count off', hence 'clear-cut, crisp, distinct, legible'.

history.meaning: exact count/reading → crisp, clear, sharp, legible

шаг.etymology: Inherited from East Slavic (attested in Old East Slavic derivatives such as сягати / шагати), from Proto-Slavic *sęgъ / *šagъ ('stride, reach, pace'), related by ablaut and expressive initial s-/š- variation to сягать ('to reach') and сажень ('fathom').
шаг.notes: In the genitive singular after kaksi/два, три, четыре, stress shifts to the ending: **два шага́**, **полшага́**, whereas ordinary genitive singular is **ша́га**.

шагать.etymology: Imperfective verb formed with the suffix -ать from шаг ('step, pace, stride'), from East Slavic шагъ.

шалить.etymology: Derived from шаль / шальной ('folly, madness; wild, crazy'), from Proto-Slavic *šalь / *šaliti ('to rage, act madly, fool around').

history.meaning: to rage, act foolishly, play pranks

шальной.etymology: Adjective formed with -ной from шаль ('folly, craze, caprice'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *šalь ('frenzy, madness, folly').

шампанское.etymology: Substantivized neuter adjective (from шампанское вино 'Champagne wine'), borrowed in the 18th century from French (vin de) Champagne, named after the historical province of Champagne in northeastern France (from Late Latin campānia 'open country, level field', from campus 'field').

шанс.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century from French chance ('luck, opportunity, fall of the dice'), from Old French cheance, from Vulgar Latin *cadentia ('a falling, the way dice fall'), derived from Latin cadere ('to fall').

шантаж.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century from French chantage ('extortion, blackmail'), derived from chanter ('to sing', in French argot faire chanter quelqu'un 'to make someone sing, extort money by threat of exposure').

шарада.etymology: Borrowed from French charade ('syllable-guessing word riddle'), borrowed from Occitan charrada ('chatter, idle talk, conversation'), from charrar ('to chatter').

шарманка.etymology: Named in Russian after the opening words of the popular 18th-century French song «Charmante Catherine» ('Charming Catherine', from French charmante 'charming'), which was one of the first tunes played on street barrel organs in Russia.

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: шарманка

шастать.etymology: East Slavic verb of onomatopoeic origin (compare шасть! 'swish!, rustle!'), originally imitating the rustling sound of moving through dry grass or grain, hence 'to prowl, gad about, pace back and forth'.

шафран.etymology: Borrowed via German Safran / Italian zafferano / Old French safran from Medieval Latin safranum, ultimately from Arabic زَعْفَرَان (zaʿfarān, 'saffron').

швед.etymology: Borrowed via Polish Szwed or Middle Low German Swede ('Swede'), ultimately from Old Swedish svear ('the Swedes').

шедевр.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century from French chef-d'œuvre ('masterpiece'), literally 'head/principal work', originally a medieval guild term for the piece of work a journeyman craftsman had to submit to the guild masters to attain the rank of master (compounded from chef 'head, chief', de 'of', and œuvre 'work', from Latin opera).

rootFamily.gloss: chef, boss (from the same French element chef)

шепнуть.etymology: Semelfactive perfective formed with the suffix -нуть from шептать ('to whisper', inherited from Old East Slavic шьпътати, from Proto-Slavic *šьpъtati).

шептать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic шьпътати ('to whisper'), from Proto-Slavic *šьpъtati, derived from onomatopoeic *šьpъtъ (Russian шёпот 'whisper'), imitating hushed sibilant speech.

шептаться.etymology: Reciprocal/reflexive form of шептать ('to whisper', from Proto-Slavic *šьpъtati) formed with the enclitic -ся.

шестеро.etymology: Collective numeral inherited from Old East Slavic шестеро, from Proto-Slavic *šestero ('group of six'), derived from *šestь ('six').

шестнадцать.etymology: Contracted from the Old East Slavic numeral phrase шесть на десяте ('six upon ten'), from Proto-Slavic *šestь na desęte.

шесть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic шесть, from Proto-Slavic *šestь ('six'), continuing Proto-Indo-European *swéḱs (cognate with Latin sex, English six, and Lithuanian šeši).

шеф.etymology: Шеф was borrowed from French chef, meaning a head or chief. Vasmer dates its Russian use to Peter the Great’s time and records an older military sense, a regimental commander. Its use for a boss or head chef continues that idea of being in charge.

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: шеф

шеф.notes:
- Colloquial address for a boss, or for a waiter, taxi driver or shop worker.
- In the sense 'chef' it is usually **шеф-повар**.

шеф-повар.etymology: Compound culinary noun joining шеф ('chief, head', borrowed from French chef, from Latin caput 'head', modelled on French chef de cuisine) + повар ('cook', native Slavic noun built on по- + варить 'to boil, cook').

history.meaning: chief + cook → head chef, executive chef

шикарно.etymology: Adverb formed from шикарный ('chic, splendid, luxurious'), derived from шик ('chic, style', borrowed from French chic).

шикарный.etymology: Formed in Russian from шик ('elegance, style, flair', borrowed from French chic) + the pseudo-French expressive suffix -арный.

шиковать.etymology: Formed in Russian from шик ('chic, ostentation, luxury', from French chic) + the verbal suffix -овать.

history.meaning: to live it up, flaunt wealth

шинковать.etymology: Borrowed via Polish szynkować / siekać or Ukrainian шинкувати, from Middle High German schinken / schenken ('to cut into slices, slice meat or cabbage').

шинковка.etymology: Verbal and instrument noun formed with the suffix -ка from шинковать ('to shred, chop cabbage or vegetables finely').

шипучка.etymology: Colloquial noun formed with the suffix -ка from шипучий ('fizzy, effervescent, hissing'), derived from шипеть ('to hiss, fizz', of onomatopoeic Proto-Slavic origin *šipěti).

шире.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic шире, comparative degree of широкий ('wide, broad') and широко ('widely'), formed directly from the root шир- (without the positive suffix -ок-) + comparative suffix -е (from Proto-Slavic *širje).

шишка.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *šišьka ('pine cone, lump, bump, tuft'); the colloquial sense 'big shot, boss' arose from the idiom держаться как шишка на ровном месте or from the lead haulers (шишка) in a barge-hauler (бурлак) team.

шкатулка.etymology: Borrowed in the seventeenth or eighteenth century via Polish szkatułka (diminutive of szkatuła) from Medieval/Italian scatola ('box, small chest, casket').

шкафчик.etymology: Diminutive formed with the suffix -чик from шкаф ('cupboard, wardrobe, cabinet'), borrowed via Polish szafa / Swedish skåp / Low German schap ('cupboard').

шкет.etymology: Colloquial word from 19th-century Russian traders' and sailors' argot (originally 'boy, apprentice'), of uncertain origin—variously connected by etymologists with Italian schietto ('simple, unadorned, young'), dialectal шкапенёк, or Baltic/Finno-Ugric forms.

школа.etymology: Borrowed via Polish szkoła from Latin schola ('school, lecture, scholarly leisure'), from Ancient Greek σχολή ('leisure, spare time devoted to learning, philosophical discussion, school').

школьница.etymology: Feminine counterpart of школьник ('schoolboy, pupil'), formed with -ница from школа ('school', borrowed via Polish szkoła from Latin schola and Ancient Greek σχολή skholḗ).

шкура.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic скура / шкура ('animal hide, pelt, skin'), related to кора ('bark, rind, peel', from Proto-Slavic *skora / *kora, from PIE *(s)ker- 'to cut, strip off').

шлагбаум.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era from German Schlagbaum ('turnpike, boom barrier', literally 'strike-tree / falling beam'), a compound of schlagen ('to strike, fall') + Baum ('tree, beam').

шлем.etymology: Adopted via Old Church Slavonic шлѣмъ ('helmet', replacing native East Slavic pleophonic шеломъ in standard Russian), from Proto-Slavic *šelmъ, an early borrowing from Proto-Germanic *helmaz ('helmet, protective head-covering', the ancestor of English helm / helmet).

шляпа.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic шляпа, borrowed early from German (Bavarian/Middle High German) Schlappe 'soft cap or hat with a wide floppy brim'.
шляпа.notes: Шляпа refers specifically to a hat with a brim; a knitted winter cap or brimless hat is шапка.

шляпка.etymology: Diminutive formed with the suffix -ка from шляпа ('hat'), borrowed from Middle High German slappe / German Schlappe ('hood, soft brimmed hat, cap').

history.meaning: little hat, lady's hat; mushroom cap; nail head

шляться.etymology: Colloquial verb of expressive Slavic origin, connected by Vasmer with шлык / шлындать ('to loaf, gad about') or Polish szlać się / ślać ('to wander, trudge').

history.meaning: to roam, gad about, loaf around

шнапс.etymology: Borrowed from German Schnaps ('strong distilled spirit, schnapps, mouthful'), from Low German snaps ('quick gulp, mouthful', related to schnappen 'to snap, swallow quickly').

шнур.etymology: Borrowed via Polish sznur from Middle High German snuor / German Schnur ('twisted cord, string, line', cognate with English snare).

шоколад.etymology: Borrowed in the early 18th century via German Schokolade and French chocolat from Spanish chocolate, which was adopted in 16th-century colonial Mexico from Classical Nahuatl xocolātl (a cacao beverage).

шорты.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English shorts ('short trousers'), plural of short (from Old English sceort).

шотландский.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -ский from Шотландия ('Scotland'), borrowed via German Schottland ('land of the Scots').

шоу-бизнес.etymology: Borrowed in the late 20th century from English show business ('the entertainment industry', a compound of show + business).

шпаргалка.etymology: Borrowed in nineteenth-century school and seminary slang from Polish szpargał ('old scrap of paper, scribbled sheet') + Russian suffix -ка, traced via Latin sparganum to Ancient Greek σπάργανον ('swaddling band, strip of cloth or paper').

шпинат.etymology: Borrowed via German Spinat (and Polish szpinak) from Medieval Latin spinatum, ultimately from Arabic إِسْفَانَاخ (ʾisfānāḵ) and Persian اسپناخ (aspanāx, 'spinach').

шприц.etymology: Borrowed from German Spritze ('syringe, squirt gun'), derived from spritzen ('to squirt, spray, inject').

шрам.etymology: Borrowed via Polish szram / szrama ('slash, scar') from Middle High German schram / German Schramme ('long scratch, slash wound, scar').

штора.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century via German Store ('window blind, roller shade, curtain') from French store ('window shade, blind'), from Latin storea ('woven mat of rush or straw').

шторм.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era from Dutch storm or Low German storm ('tempest, gale at sea'), from Proto-Germanic *sturmaz ('storm').

штука.etymology: Borrowed via Polish sztuka ('piece, item; work of art, trick') from Middle High German stucke / German Stück ('piece, bit, individual item').

штучка.etymology: Diminutive formed with the suffix -ка from штука ('piece, item; trick'), borrowed via Polish sztuka ('piece; art; trick') from Middle High German stücke / German Stück ('piece, bit').

шуба.etymology: Attested in Old East Slavic шуба since the 14th century; borrowed via Middle High German schūbe /ube ('long outer garment, fur-lined coat') and Italian giubba from Arabic جُبَّة (jubba, 'long outer wool garment').

шумно.etymology: Adverbial and impersonal predicate form in -о of шумный ('noisy, loud'), derived from шум ('noise, rustle, din', from Old East Slavic шумъ and Proto-Slavic *šumъ).

шуруп.etymology: Borrowed via Polish szruba / śruba or Ukrainian шуруп from Middle High German schrūbe / Low German schruve (German Schraube, 'screw').

шутить.etymology: Derived from шут ('jester, fool, joker'), inherited from Old East Slavic шутъ (Proto-Slavic *šutъ, originally 'hornless, cropped, foolish, jester-like'; compare Lithuanian šiautas 'hornless' and Bulgarian шут 'hornless; jester').

шутка.etymology: Formed with the suffix -ка from шут ('jester, buffoon, fool', attested in Old East Slavic шутъ) and шутить ('to joke, jest'). The deeper origin of Proto-Slavic *šutъ is debated: Vasmer connects it with South Slavic *šutъ ('hornless, cropped, bald, foolish') and Lithuanian šiaũštis / šùtas, referring to the shaved head or comic appearance of medieval jesters.

шутник.etymology: Formed with the agent suffix -ник from шутить ('to joke, jest') / шут ('jester, buffoon', inherited from Old East Slavic шутъ, from Proto-Slavic *šutъ).

шёпот.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic шепътъ ('whisper, rustle'), from Proto-Slavic *šepъtъ, formed with the sound-noun suffix *-ъtъ (as in грохот, топот) on the onomatopoeic root *šep- imitating hushed, sibilant breathing.
шёпот.notes: In the instrumental singular **шёпотом** it functions as an adverb meaning 'in a whisper'.

щадить.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic щадѣти ('to spare, have mercy, save'), from Proto-Slavic *ščęděti ('to spare, be thrifty with'; compare native East Slavic скудный 'scant, meager').

щедрость.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic щедрость ('mercy, bounty, generosity'), formed with -ость from щедрый ('bountiful, merciful, generous', from Proto-Slavic *ščedrъ).

щека.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic щека ('cheek, jaw; steep rocky riverbank'). Vasmer notes that its deeper pre-Slavic etymology is uncertain, comparing either Proto-Slavic *ščeka with expressive words for jaws/biting or rocks.
щека.notes: Accusative singular shifts stress to the stem (**за́ щеку** or **в щёку**), and nominative plural is **щёки** (genitive plural **щёк**).

щелчок.etymology: Formed with the single-action noun suffix -ок from щёлкать ('to click, snap, flick', with к → ч before -ок), built on the onomatopoeic Slavic root *ščьlk- imitating a sharp click or snap.

history.meaning: to click, snap → a click, snap, flick

щепотка.etymology: Diminutive in -ка of щепоть ('the thumb and two index/middle fingers brought together; a pinch'), derived from щипать / щепать ('to pinch, pluck, split off a small splinter').

history.meaning: three fingers pinched together; a pinch

щиток.etymology: Diminutive in -ок of щит ('shield, protective board'), inherited from Old East Slavic щитъ and Proto-Slavic *ščitъ ('shield, board', cognate with Latin scūtum 'shield'). In modern technical Russian, щиток denotes a small protective panel, switchboard, or fuse box.

history.meaning: shield → small shield, dashboard, fuse box

щучий.etymology: Possessive/relational adjective formed from щука ('pike', a predatory freshwater fish) with palatalization of к > ч before the suffix -ий. Inherited from Old East Slavic щука, from Proto-Slavic *ščuka ('pike', compare Polish szczupak / szczuka). Famous in Russian folklore from the fairy-tale formula **по щучьему велению, по моему хотенью** ('at the pike's command, at my desire', i.e., 'as if by magic').

щёлк.etymology: Onomatopoeic verbal interjection imitating the sharp sound of a lock clicking, fingers snapping, or a switch toggling, extracted from the stem of щёлкать / щёлкнуть ('to click, snap').

щёлкнуть.etymology: Semelfactive perfective verb in -нуть from щёлкать ('to click, snap'), built on the expressive onomatopoeic Slavic root *ščьlk- imitating a sharp metallic or wooden click.

history.meaning: to click repeatedly → to give a single click

эвакуировать.etymology: Borrowed from German evakuieren or French évacuer ('to empty out, evacuate'), from Latin evacuare ('to empty, clear out'), from e- ('out') + vacuus ('empty').

history.meaning: to evacuate; to tow away a vehicle

эгоизм.etymology: Borrowed from French égoïsme ('selfishness, self-interest'), coined in the 18th century from Latin ego ('I') + the suffix -isme.

эгоист.etymology: Borrowed from French égoïste ('selfish person, egoist'), formed from Latin ego ('I') + the agent suffix -iste.

эй.etymology: Primary vocalic call interjection used across Slavic and Indo-European languages to attract someone's attention from a distance ('hey!, hallo!').

экземпляр.etymology: Borrowed via German Exemplar or Polish egzemplarz from Latin exemplar ('model, pattern, transcript, copy'), from exemplum ('sample, example').

экзотический.etymology: Borrowed via French exotique or German exotisch (with Russian suffix -еский) from Latin exoticus, from Ancient Greek ἐξωτικός (exōtikós, 'foreign, from the outside'), from ἔξω (éxō, 'outside').

эклер.etymology: Borrowed from French éclair ('choux pastry finger filled with cream and topped with icing', literally 'flash of lightning'), attested in this culinary sense since the 1860s (so called either because it is eaten in a flash or because its glaze gleams).

history.meaning: flash of lightning; cream-filled choux pastry

экономика.etymology: Borrowed via German Ökonomik / Polish ekonomika from Latin oeconomica, from Ancient Greek οἰκονομική (oikonomikḗ, 'art of household management'), from οἶκος (oîkos, 'house') + νόμος (nómos, 'custom, law, management').

экономия.etymology: Borrowed via Polish ekonomia or German Ökonomie from Latin oeconomia, from Ancient Greek οἰκονομία (oikonomía, 'household management, thrift, stewardship').

экономно.etymology: Adverb formed from экономный ('thrifty, economical'), derived from экономия / эконом ('steward, housekeeper, thrifty person', from Ancient Greek οἰκονόμος).

экспедиция.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via Polish ekspedycja / German Expedition from Latin expedītiō ('a campaign, journey of exploration, dispatch'), from expedīre ('to free the feet from fetters, make ready, dispatch', built on ex- 'out' + pēs, pedis 'foot').

history.meaning: to make ready, dispatch → campaign, expedition

экспериментировать.etymology: Borrowed from German experimentieren ('to experiment'), derived from Latin experimentum ('trial, proof, experiment', from experiri 'to try, test').

эксперт.etymology: Borrowed from French expert or German Experte, from Latin expertus ('tried, proved, experienced'), past participle of experiri ('to try thoroughly, test').

экспертиза.etymology: Borrowed from French expertise ('expert assessment, appraisal') or German Expertise, derived from expert ('specialist, expert').

экстракт.etymology: Borrowed via German Extrakt from Medieval Latin extractum ('concentrated essence drawn out'), neuter past participle of Latin extrahere ('to draw out, extract').

электрик.etymology: Borrowed from French électrique or formed in Russian from электричество ('electricity', ultimately from New Latin electricus and Ancient Greek ἤλεκτρον ḗlektron 'amber'), denoting a specialist in electrical wiring.

элементарно.etymology: Adverb formed from элементарный ('elementary, basic, simple'), from Latin elementarius ('belonging to rudiments or first principles').

элементарный.etymology: Borrowed via German elementar or Polish elementarny from Latin elementarius ('relating to first principles or elements'), derived from elementum ('first principle, basic component').

элита.etymology: Borrowed from French élite ('the chosen, the best part'), substantivized feminine past participle in Old French of élire ('to choose, elect', from Latin eligere).

элитный.etymology: Relational and qualitative adjective formed with the suffix -ный from элита ('elite', from French élite).

эмоция.etymology: Borrowed via French émotion (and Polish emocja) from Middle French esmotion ('stirring up, agitation of mind'), from Latin emovere ('to move out, stir up, agitate').

энергичный.etymology: Formed with the adjective suffix -ичный (after German energisch or French énergique) from энергия ('energy', from Ancient Greek ἐνέργεια).

энергия.etymology: Borrowed via German Energie or Polish energia from Late Latin energia, from Ancient Greek ἐνέργεια (enérgeia, 'action, operation, vigor'), coined by Aristotle from ἐνεργός (energós, 'active, at work', from ἐν 'in' + ἔργον 'work').

этап.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th–19th centuries from French étape ('stopping place for troops on the march, supply depot, stage of a journey'), from Old French estaple ('market, depot', from Middle Dutch stapel).

этикетка.etymology: Formed with -ка from этикет, borrowed from French etiquette, which originally meant a small paper slip or ticket attached to a bag or bottle to show its contents before also coming to mean court protocol.

cognates.meaning: paper slip, ticket (from Old French estiquette)

этикетка.notes: Russian splits the two senses cleanly: этикет is social etiquette, while этикетка is a physical label.

это.etymology: Formed in East Slavic by combining the deictic interjection/particle э- ('eh, look here!') with то ('that', neuter singular of тот, from Proto-Slavic *to and Proto-Indo-European *tód). Functions both as the neuter demonstrative pronoun ('this, that') and as the invariant copular presenter ('this is..., it is...').

history.meaning: look here + that → this, that; it is

эфирный.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -ный from эфир ('ether, upper air; volatile essential oil; broadcast airwaves'), borrowed via Latin aether from Ancient Greek αἰθήρ (aithḗr, 'pure upper air, clear sky').

эффектно.etymology: Adverb formed from эффектный ('striking, spectacular, impressive'), derived from эффект ('effect, impression', from Latin effectus).

эффектный.etymology: Adjective formed with the suffix -ный from эффект ('effect, striking impression'), borrowed via German Effekt / French effet from Latin effectus ('accomplishment, result, effect', from efficere).

эхо.etymology: Borrowed via Latin ēchō (and Western European languages) from Ancient Greek ἠχώ ('echo, reflected sound'), related to ἦχος ('sound, ringing') and personified in Greek myth as the mountain nymph Echo.

эхолот.etymology: Borrowed from German Echolot ('echo sounder, sonar depth-finder'), a compound of Echo ('echo', from Ancient Greek ἠχώ) + Lot ('plummet, sounding lead').

юбка.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century via Polish jupka (diminutive of jupa 'short jacket, bodice, skirt') and Middle High German juppe / joppe from Italian giubba, ultimately from Arabic جُبَّة (jubba, 'long outer garment'; a doublet of шуба).

ювелир.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era from German Juwelier or Dutch juwelier ('jeweler'), ultimately from Old French joel ('jewel, ornament, plaything', related to jeu 'game, play', from Latin jocus).

ювелирный.etymology: Relational and qualitative adjective formed with the suffix -ный from ювелир ('jeweler').

югославский.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -ский from Югославия ('Yugoslavia'), coined from South Slavic jug ('south', Proto-Slavic *jugъ) + Славия ('land of the Slavs').

южный.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -ный from юг ('south'), borrowed from Old Church Slavonic югъ (replacing native East Slavic угъ, preserved in ужин), from Proto-Slavic *jugъ ('south, warm wind').

юмор.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century via English humour (and German Humor) from Old French humor and Latin humor / umor ('moisture, bodily fluid'; in medieval medicine, the four bodily humors were held to determine temperament and wit).

юноша.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic юноша ('young man, youth', with South Slavic initial ю- corresponding to East Slavic уноша), formed with the suffix -оша from юнъ ('young', from Proto-Slavic *junъ, cognate with Latin iuvenis and English young).

юридически.etymology: Adverb formed from юридический ('legal, juridical'), borrowed via German juridisch or Polish jurydyczny from Medieval Latin iuridicus ('relating to the administration of justice', from ius, iuris 'law, right' + dicere 'to say, pronounce').

юридический.etymology: Borrowed via German juristisch / Medieval Latin iūridicus from Latin iūridicus ('relating to the administration of justice, legal'), a compound of iūs, iūris ('law, right') + dīcere ('to speak, pronounce judgment').

юрист.etymology: Borrowed via German Jurist from Medieval Latin iūrista ('expert in law, jurist'), built on Latin iūs, iūris ('law, right').

я.etymology: An inherited Slavic first-person pronoun. Vasmer records both язъ and я in an Old Russian document of 1130 and compares Old Church Slavonic азъ. He also compares more distant relatives such as Latin ego. Some details of the sound changes, including the loss of the final consonant, remain disputed.

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: я

яблоко.etymology: An inherited Slavic word for apple. Vasmer compares the Slavic family with Baltic and Germanic relatives, including the older Germanic word behind English apple. Similarity here reflects a shared older word family rather than borrowing from modern English.

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: яблоко

яблоко.notes: The plural is яблоки; the genitive plural is яблок. Both keep the stress on the first syllable. Глазное яблоко means eyeball.

яблочко.etymology: Diminutive formed with the suffix -ко from яблоко ('apple', inherited from Old East Slavic яблъко, from Proto-Slavic *ablъko).
